What history is.back: Greek: **inquiry** — finding out by asking. Herodotus's word, 430s BC.

What history is.front: The past and history: the difference
What history is.back: The **past** is everything that happened, mostly unrecorded. **History** is what can be said about it **from the evidence that survives**.
The human past **before writing** (writing begins about **3200 BC** in Mesopotamia and Egypt). Studied from bones, tools, DNA and the ground.

The world at a glance.front: Why do the first civilisations all sit on rivers?
The world at a glance.back: Flooding rivers fed farmland: **Tigris-Euphrates, Nile, Indus, Yellow River**.
The belt of grassland across Eurasia from Hungary to Mongolia — **the highway of horse peoples**.

The world at a glance.front: How does the Mercator map mislead?
The world at a glance.back: It keeps directions true for sailors but **swells land near the poles**: Africa is about **14 times** the size of Greenland, though they look similar.

Evidence: primary and secondary sources.back: Evidence **from the time being studied**: a letter, coin, inscription, skeleton.
An account **written later**, using primary sources: an interpretation.

Evidence: primary and secondary sources.front: Five questions to ask of any source
Evidence: primary and secondary sources.back: **Who** made it? **When?** **For whom?** **Why?** **What does it leave out?**

Primary source: Herodotus says why he wr.back: Greek of Halicarnassus, born about **484 BC**; wrote the *Histories* (about 430 BC) on the **Greek–Persian wars**. The father of history.

Primary source: Herodotus says why he wr.front: Herodotus's two purposes, in his opening
Primary source: Herodotus says why he wr.back: That deeds **not be forgotten**, and **"especially that the causes may be remembered"** — why, not just what.

Counting years: BC, AD, BCE and CE.back: Monk in Rome who in **AD 525** worked out counting years **from the birth of Christ**.
**The same numbers** as BC / AD, with religiously neutral labels.
Counted from the **Hijra**, AD **622**; lunar years.

Dating without writing: layers, tree rin.back: Dating by layers: **newer on top of older**. Gives order, not years.
Dating by **tree-ring** patterns; reaches back about **12,000 years** in Europe.

Dating without writing: layers, tree rin.front: Radiocarbon dating: how and how far
Dating without writing: layers, tree rin.back: Carbon-14 in once-living things decays with a **half-life of about 5,730 years**; works to about **50,000 years**; must be **calibrated**. Willard **Libby**, late 1940s.

Why things happen: cause, consequence an.front: A trigger is not a cause — example
Why things happen: cause, consequence an.back: The assassination of **Franz Ferdinand** (28 June **1914**) triggered the First World War; alliances, arms races and nationalism were the causes.
**Chance**: things that could have gone otherwise — weather, illness, a late message.
Knowing the ending makes it look **inevitable**; people at the time faced an **open future**.

When historians disagree.back: **New evidence**, **different questions**, **thin or one-sided sources**, and **their own times**.

When historians disagree.front: The fall of Rome: the four readings
When historians disagree.back: **Decline from within** (Gibbon), **murder from outside**, **transformation** not fall, and **collapse after all** (Ward-Perkins, from archaeology).
All good history is **revised from evidence**; propaganda **denies** evidence.

Deep time: the Earth and the first homin.back: Humans and their extinct relatives **after the split from the chimpanzee line**, about **7–6 million years ago**.
Chad, about **7 million years ago**: perhaps the earliest hominin.
**No** — we share a **common ancestor** (and about 98–99% of our DNA).

Standing up: the australopithecines.back: *Australopithecus afarensis*, **Hadar, Ethiopia, 1974**; about **3.2 million years** old; walked upright and still climbed.
Tanzania, about **3.66 million years** ago; found 1978 (Mary Leakey): the oldest direct evidence of **upright walking**.
South Africa, **1924**, Raymond **Dart**: *Australopithecus africanus*; his claim that **Africa is the cradle of humankind** was rejected for decades, then proved right.

The first tools.back: The first stone-flake tools, from about **2.6 million years ago** (Gona, Ethiopia); named after **Olduvai Gorge**.
Teardrop tool worked on both faces, from about **1.76 million years ago**; used for over **a million years**.
"Handy man", about **2.4–1.6 million years ago**; the first species placed in *Homo*.

Homo erectus and the first journeys out.back: From about **1.9 million years ago**; human body proportions; **the first hominin to leave Africa**.
Georgia: hominin skulls about **1.8 million years** old — early humans already outside Africa.
"The hobbit": a tiny hominin on the island of **Flores**, alive until about **50,000 years ago**.

Fire.back: South Africa: burnt bone and ash deep in a cave, about **1 million years** old — early evidence of fire use.
**Cooking**, **warmth**, **protection** from predators, **light** (time to talk and teach), and **tools**.

Our cousins: Neanderthals, Denisovans an.back: Europe and western Asia, about **400,000–40,000 years ago**; brains as large as ours; named after a valley in Germany (1856).
A human group known mainly **from DNA** in a finger bone from Denisova Cave, Siberia (**2010**).

Our cousins: Neanderthals, Denisovans an.front: How much Neanderthal is in us?
Our cousins: Neanderthals, Denisovans an.back: People outside Africa carry about **1–2% Neanderthal DNA**, from interbreeding.
Rising Star cave, South Africa: small-brained, yet alive **335,000–236,000 years ago**.

Homo sapiens in Africa.back: Morocco: the oldest *Homo sapiens* fossils, about **300,000 years** old (dated 2017).

Homo sapiens in Africa.front: Why do Africans hold the most human genetic diversity?
Homo sapiens in Africa.back: Humanity **grew up in Africa**; those who left were a **small sample** of it.
The **modern body** came by about 300,000–100,000 years ago; **symbols, art and ornaments** appeared gradually, first in Africa.

The first symbols: Blombos and the beads.back: Western Cape, South Africa: **engraved ochre** and **shell beads**, about **75,000 years** old; a paint workshop about **100,000**.

The first symbols: Blombos and the beads.front: Why a bead matters more than a hand-axe
The first symbols: Blombos and the beads.back: A bead is useful only because **people agree what it means** — shared symbols are the root of language, ritual, law and trade.

Out of Africa: the great dispersal.back: About **70,000–50,000 years ago**, the small population from which **almost everyone outside Africa** descends left Africa.
The strait at the mouth of the **Red Sea**: the proposed **southern route** out of Africa.

Out of Africa: the great dispersal.front: Modern humans reached Europe by about…

The Ice Age world.back: The coldest point of the last Ice Age, about **26,000–20,000 years ago**; seas about **120 m lower**.
The Ice Age land bridge between **Siberia and Alaska**.
The warm, stable period since about **11,700 years ago**, in which farming became possible.
Giant Ice Age animals — mammoths, woolly rhinos, giant sloths, giant kangaroos — mostly gone by **10,000 years ago**.

Into Australia and the Americas.back: Certainly by about **50,000 years ago**; possibly **65,000** (Madjedbebe, debated). The first known **sea crossings**.
New South Wales: remains about **42,000 years** old, including the world's **oldest known cremation**.
Chile, about **14,500 years ago**: the site that ended "Clovis first".
New Mexico: human footprints dated about **23,000–21,000 years ago** (debated).

How hunter-gatherers lived.front: The size of a hunter-gatherer band
How hunter-gatherers lived.back: About **20–50 people**, within a wider network of a few hundred to a thousand.
Marshall **Sahlins** (1966): hunter-gatherers worked few hours and had much leisure. Later work: **longer hours than he said; the truth in between**.

How hunter-gatherers lived.front: Were all hunter-gatherers mobile and equal?
How hunter-gatherers lived.back: **No** — on the rich Pacific coast of North America they lived in **permanent villages**, ranked by wealth, with slaves.

Cave art and the first figurines.back: Indonesia: paintings at least **45,500–51,200 years** old — older than any in Europe.
France, about **36,000 years** old: lions, rhinos, horses with shading and perspective.
Hohlenstein-Stadel, Germany, about **40,000 years** old: a man with a lion's head, in mammoth ivory — an imagined being.
**Hunting magic**, **shamanism** (Lewis-Williams, from San rock art), **storytelling or marking territory** — no one knows.

Connections: the world at the end of the.back: Levant, about **12,000 years ago**: hunter-gatherers in **stone villages** harvesting wild cereals — on the edge of farming.
Japan: hunter-gatherers making some of the **world's oldest pottery** (over **15,000 years** old).

Connections: the world at the end of the.front: World population at the end of the Ice Age
Connections: the world at the end of the.back: Perhaps **a few million** — estimates range from about 1 to 10 million.

Map: the world as the ice melted, about.back: A last cold snap, about **10,900–9700 BC**, before the warm Holocene began.
About **9700 BC**: the stable warm period we still live in begins, and with it the age of farming.
Land joining **Britain to the Continent** across the North Sea; drowned in stages, mostly gone by about **6000 BC**.

Map: the world as the ice melted, about.front: How long from the first fields to the first cities in the Near East?
Map: the world as the ice melted, about.back: About **5,000 years** — longer than from the pyramids to today.

Why people started farming: the rival ex.front: Why did farming begin only after the Ice Age?
Why people started farming: the rival ex.back: Ice Age climates were **unstable and low in CO2**; the **Holocene's stable warmth** made farming possible on several continents within a few thousand years.
Robert **Braidwood**, 1950s: farming began in the **uplands** where wild wheat grew, not in the river valleys.
Jacques **Cauvin**: a change in **religion** came before farming; Göbekli Tepe seemed to support it.

The Natufians and the first farms of the.back: Levant, about **12,500–9500 BC**: settled hunter-gatherers harvesting **wild cereals**; baked a flatbread at Shubayqa 1 about **12,400 BC**.

The Natufians and the first farms of the.front: How did harvesting turn wild wheat into a crop?
The Natufians and the first farms of the.back: Sickle harvesting and replanting selected mutants with a **non-shattering ear**, which keep their seeds on the stalk.
The Near East's first crops: **emmer, einkorn, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch, flax**.
Arc from the **Levant through south-east Turkey to the Zagros**; name coined by James Henry **Breasted**, 1916.

Göbekli Tepe: monuments before farming.back: Near Şanlıurfa, Turkey, about **9500–8000 BC**: enclosures of carved **T-shaped pillars** over 5 m tall, built before full domestication.
Klaus **Schmidt**: a ritual centre with **no houses**. Later excavation found **houses, cisterns and grinding stones**: a settlement with monuments. Still debated.
One of the **Taş Tepeler** sites near Göbekli Tepe, dug since **2019**: a room with heads and figures carved from the rock.

Jericho and Çatalhöyük: the first big vi.back: Stone tower about **8.5 m** high with an inner staircase, about **8300–8000 BC**; dug by Kathleen **Kenyon**. Defence, flood control or ritual — unsettled.
Konya plain, Turkey, about **7100–5950 BC**: packed mud-brick houses entered **through the roof**, dead buried under floors; **3,000–8,000** people.

Jericho and Çatalhöyük: the first big vi.front: Why is Çatalhöyük called a village, not a city?
Jericho and Çatalhöyük: the first big vi.back: It had **no palace, temple or public buildings**, and houses of **similar size**: large, but fairly **equal**.

Taming animals: dogs, sheep, goats, catt.back: The huge **wild ox**, ancestor of cattle; tamed on the upper Euphrates about **8500 BC** (zebu separately in the Indus region).
Andrew **Sherratt**, 1981: **milk, wool and traction** exploited only from about 4000–3000 BC. Milk residues show **milking was earlier**.

Taming animals: dogs, sheep, goats, catt.front: Botai horses: why don't they count as the first domestic horses?
Taming animals: dogs, sheep, goats, catt.back: Ancient DNA (2021) showed they were ancestors of **Przewalski's horse**; modern horses come from the **lower Volga–Don**, spreading after about **2200 BC**.

Taming animals: dogs, sheep, goats, catt.front: How does domestication show in animal bones?
Taming animals: dogs, sheep, goats, catt.back: Animals get **smaller**, and herds show **young males culled, females kept** — a pattern no hunter would choose.

China's two farmings: northern millet an.back: **Millet** (broomcorn and foxtail) in the dry **Yellow River** north; **rice** in the wet **Yangtze** south.
Henan, about **7000–5700 BC**: bone **flutes**, rice and millet, and one of the **oldest known alcoholic drinks**.
Middle Yellow River, about **5000–3000 BC**: painted pottery; villages like **Banpo**.

New Guinea's Kuk Swamp: farming in the h.back: Papua New Guinea highlands: an **independent** farming centre, with mounds about **5000–4400 BC** and ditched fields later; UNESCO **2008**.
Not cereals but **taro, yams, bananas** and **sugarcane**.

New Guinea's Kuk Swamp: farming in the h.front: What does New Guinea show about farming and cities?
New Guinea's Kuk Swamp: farming in the h.back: Farming **does not automatically lead to cities**: its farmers lived in villages and clans, with about **1,000 languages**.

Maize from teosinte: farming in Mesoamer.back: Wild grass of the **Balsas valley**, Mexico: the **ancestor of maize**, confirmed by genetics in **2002**.
Oaxaca cave: domestic **squash about 8000 BC** and the oldest **maize cobs, about 4300 BC**.
Mesoamerica's **maize, beans and squash**, grown together.
Soaking maize in **lime or ash water** frees **niacin** and prevents **pellagra**; maize taken abroad without it caused the disease.

The Andes and Amazonia: potatoes, llamas.back: From the **Lake Titicaca** region; domestication under way by perhaps **6000–5000 BC** (poorly dated).
Tamed from the **guanaco and vicuña** by about **4000 BC**; the llama was the Americas' only beast of burden.
"Black earth": dark Amazonian soils **enriched by long human use**.

Africa's own farmers: the green Sahara,.back: About **9000–3500 BC**: the **green Sahara**, with lakes and savanna.

Africa's own farmers: the green Sahara,.front: Africa's farming order, compared with the Near East
Africa's own farmers: the green Sahara,.back: In Africa, **herding came before planting**; pottery came before both.
Domesticated in the southern Sahara of **Mali** by about **2500 BC**; reached India by about 2000 BC.
Crops domesticated in the **Ethiopian highlands** (also noog and coffee); dates poorly known.

Farmers on the move: the Neolithic reach.back: Central Europe's first farmers, from about **5500 BC**, with **longhouses** from Hungary to the Paris basin.

Farmers on the move: the Neolithic reach.front: Did farming spread into Europe by migration or by ideas?
Farmers on the move: the Neolithic reach.back: Ancient DNA: mostly by **migration** — first farmers descended from **Anatolian farmers**, mixing slowly with hunter-gatherers.
Balochistan, Pakistan, about **7000 BC**: barley, wheat, goats, **zebu**; drilled teeth — the first known **dentistry**.
Germany, about **5000 BC**: **34** people killed with stone axes.

The price of farming: health, work and i.front: What do skeletons show about early farmers?
The price of farming: health, work and i.back: Often **shorter**, more **cavities**, more **anaemia**, childhood stress and **infection** than the foragers before them.

The price of farming: health, work and i.front: Why farm if it made people less healthy?
The price of farming: health, work and i.back: More food per acre and **higher birth rates** (the **Neolithic demographic transition**): farming groups grew and spread.
James C. **Scott**, 2017: grain could be **seen, measured and taxed**, so early states were built on it.

Copper, megaliths and the steppe: Europe.back: Bulgaria, about **4500 BC**: the **oldest large hoard of worked gold**; grave 43 shows a rich elite.
Died in the Ötztal Alps about **3300 BC**; found **1991**; carried a **copper axe**; killed by an arrow.
Steppe herders, about **3300–2600 BC**, with wagons and kurgans; their descendants' migration reshaped Europe's ancestry.
Indo-European languages spread by **steppe herders** (Gimbutas, Anthony; fits the DNA) or by **first farmers** (Renfrew, 1987). Steppe favoured for Europe; deeper roots debated.

Uruk: the first city.back: Southern Iraq; about **250 ha** and perhaps **25,000–50,000** people by **3100 BC**; temples of **Inanna** and **Anu**.
About **3200–3000 BC**: bands showing society's order up to the goddess Inanna; looted in **2003** and returned.
Mass-made crude bowls of the Uruk period, probably for **grain rations**.

Uruk: the first city.front: The Uruk expansion: colonies or copying?
Uruk: the first city.back: Algaze (1993): Uruk planted **trading colonies** for timber, metal and stone; others: northern sites **copied** Uruk. Still debated.

From tokens to cuneiform: writing in Sum.back: Wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay with a reed, from about **3300–3200 BC** at Uruk; used for about **3,000 years**.
Argued that **clay tokens** (from about 8000 BC) led through envelopes to **writing**; widely taught, also criticised.
Using a sign for its **sound**: Sumerian *ti* 'arrow' also wrote *ti* 'life'.

From tokens to cuneiform: writing in Sum.front: Behistun inscription and the decipherment of cuneiform
From tokens to cuneiform: writing in Sum.back: Darius's **three-language** inscription in Iran, copied by Henry **Rawlinson**; key to deciphering cuneiform in the **1850s**.

The Sumerian city-states: temples, ziggu.back: Sumerian for **"big man": king**; beside *en* (lord) and *ensi* (city ruler).
About **2450 BC**: **Eannatum of Lagash** defeats Umma; soldiers in a phalanx.
About **2600–2450 BC**, dug by Leonard **Woolley** 1922–34; **Puabi**, and **74** attendants in the Great Death Pit.
Stepped mud-brick temple tower built by **Ur-Nammu** about **2100 BC**: the god's house, not a tomb.

Primary source: Gilgamesh, and the wild.back: The **wild man** of the Gilgamesh epic who becomes human by eating **bread** and drinking **beer**.

Primary source: Gilgamesh, and the wild.front: What does Enkidu's taming show about Mesopotamian values?
Primary source: Gilgamesh, and the wild.back: To be human is to live in the **farmed, made world**: bread, beer, oil, cloth and the city.
**Old Babylonian** Gilgamesh tablet (about 1800 BC); translated by **Jastrow and Clay, 1920**.

Egypt unified: Naqada, Narmer and the fi.back: About **3100 BC**, found at Hierakonpolis **1897–98**: Narmer in the **white crown** of Upper Egypt and the **red crown** of Lower Egypt.
About **3300–3200 BC**, dug by Günter **Dreyer** in 1988: bone labels that may be the **earliest Egyptian writing**.

Egypt unified: Naqada, Narmer and the fi.front: Was Egypt unified by conquest or slowly?
Egypt unified: Naqada, Narmer and the fi.back: **Conquest** (the palette, the Menes tradition) or **slow merging** (Upper Egyptian culture spread north first). Many combine them.
First king in tradition (Manetho, 3rd century BC); identified with **Narmer** or **Hor-Aha**.

The Old Kingdom: the god-king and the fi.back: Egyptian **truth, justice and cosmic order**, which the king had to uphold.
Saqqara, about **2670 BC**, designed by **Imhotep**: the **oldest large stone building** in the world.
Spells carved in the pyramid of **Unas**, about **2350 BC**: the oldest large body of religious writing.
About **2181–2055 BC**: Egypt split between rival kings after the Old Kingdom.

Giza: how the Great Pyramid was built, a.back: About **146.6 m** high, about **2.3 million** blocks; Khufu reigned about **2589–2566 BC**; tallest building for over 3,800 years.
Papyri found at **Wadi al-Jarf** in **2013**: an inspector's log of moving **Tura limestone** to Giza in Khufu's reign.
Not chattel slaves: **skilled crews** plus **rotating labour duty**, fed and housed in a workers' town; perhaps **10,000–30,000** at a time.

Writing invented more than once.back: **Mesopotamia** (about 3300 BC), **China** (by about 1250 BC), **Mesoamerica** (by about 600 BC); **Egypt** probably too.
Borrowing the **idea**, not the system — as **Sequoyah** did for Cherokee, about **1821**.
Script of **Susa** and the Iranian plateau, about **3100–2900 BC**; still largely undeciphered.

The Indus cities: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro.back: The Indus civilisation at its height, about **2600–1900 BC**, over about **800,000 km²**.
A watertight brick tank about **12 by 7 m**, sealed with bitumen; probably for **ritual bathing**.

The Indus cities: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro.front: What is missing from the Indus cities?
The Indus cities: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro.back: No clear **palaces, royal tombs or great temples**, and no images of kings at war.
Indus city in Gujarat with great stone **reservoirs** and a ten-sign 'signboard'.

The Indus puzzles: an unread script and.front: Why can't the Indus script be read?
The Indus puzzles: an unread script and.back: Inscriptions average about **five signs**, and there is **no bilingual** text.

The Indus puzzles: an unread script and.front: Why did the Indus cities empty after about 1900 BC?
The Indus puzzles: an unread script and.back: Probably **several causes**: weaker monsoon, **rivers drying** (Ghaggar-Hakra), loss of trade. The Aryan invasion idea is largely abandoned.
Dried river along which many Indus sites lie; some identify it with the Rigveda's **Sarasvati**.

Before the Shang: Longshan towns, Taosi.back: Lower Yangtze, about **3300–2300 BC**: a walled city, great **dams**, and jade **cong** and **bi**; UNESCO 2019.
Henan, about **1900–1500 BC**: palaces, a road grid and **bronze ritual vessels** — the strongest candidate for China's first state.
Right place and time (many Chinese archaeologists say yes), but **no writing names it**; the Xia texts are 1,000+ years later. Unsettled.
Soil **pounded in layers** between boards: the walls of Longshan and later Chinese towns.

Caral and Norte Chico: the first towns o.back: Supe valley, Peru, in use by about **2600 BC**; excavated by Ruth **Shady** from 1994; **platform mounds** and **sunken circular plazas**.
Coastal Norte Chico site with platform mounds from about **3000 BC**.
Moseley's **maritime** thesis (anchovies, sardines) plus **irrigated cotton** and crops; the role of **maize** is disputed.

Caral and Norte Chico: the first towns o.front: What is unusual about Norte Chico among early civilisations?
Caral and Norte Chico: the first towns o.back: **No pottery, no writing**, and **no clear signs of war**.

Sargon of Akkad: the first empire.back: Reigned about **2334–2279 BC**; *Šarru-kīn*, "the true king"; defeated **Lugal-zage-si** and united Sumer and beyond.
Sargon's capital, which named **Akkad** and **Akkadian**; **never found**.
Sargon's daughter, high priestess at **Ur**; hymns to **Inanna** attributed to her — the **first named author**, if the attribution holds.
Sargon's grandson, about **2254–2218 BC**: "King of the Four Quarters", **made himself a god**; Victory Stele in the Louvre.

The crisis around 2200 BC: drought, the.back: Drier, cooler spell from about **2200 BC**; the start of the **Meghalayan age** (2018).

The crisis around 2200 BC: drought, the.front: Did drought destroy Akkad and the Old Kingdom?
The crisis around 2200 BC: drought, the.back: Harvey **Weiss** (1993): yes, decisively. Others: **one stress among many** — revolts, Gutians, strong governors. Finer dating would settle it.
About **2100 BC**: the **oldest surviving law code**, with fines in silver for injuries.
**2004 BC**: Elamites sack Ur and take **Ibbi-Sin**; ends the Third Dynasty of Ur.

Connections: the world of 2000 BC.back: Mesopotamian name for the **Indus**; with **Dilmun** (Bahrain) and **Magan** (Oman) in the Gulf trade.
Deep-blue stone from **Badakhshan**, Afghanistan, found in Ur's royal tombs and Egyptian graves.
Syria, about **2400–2300 BC**, found **1974–76**: records of trade with Mari and other cities.

Map: the world around 2000 BC.back: Copper with about **a tenth part tin**. Tin was rare, so bronze needed **long-distance trade**.
Town in central Anatolia where **merchants from Ashur** traded tin and cloth, about **1950–1750 BC**; over 20,000 of their letters survive.

Map: the world around 2000 BC.front: Why are Near Eastern dates before 1400 BC uncertain?
Map: the world around 2000 BC.back: The king lists cannot yet be tied exactly to astronomy or tree rings, so scholars use **competing chronologies** (high, middle, low); dates can be **off by decades**.

Horse, chariot and the Indo-European lan.back: Southern Urals, about **2100–1800 BC**: the first **spoked-wheel chariots**, buried with warriors.
The lost ancestor language of Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Germanic and the rest; kinship noticed by **William Jones, 1786**.

Steppe: spread by **Yamnaya herders** after about 3300 BC (backed by ancient DNA). Anatolian: spread with **the first farmers** after about 7000 BC (Renfrew). Most now favour the steppe for most branches.
Bred on the **lower Volga–Don steppe about 2200 BC** (ancient DNA, 2021); spread across Eurasia within centuries.

Egypt's Middle Kingdom, about 2055–1650.back: Ruler of **Thebes** who **reunited Egypt about 2055 BC**, starting the Middle Kingdom.
12th-Dynasty king, about **1870–1831 BC**; conquered Lower Nubia and built forts at the **Second Cataract**.
Middle Kingdom story of an official who **flees to the Levant** and longs to be buried in Egypt; a classic of Middle Egyptian.

Hammurabi and Old Babylon.back: Amorite king of **Babylon**, about **1792–1750 BC**; conquered Larsa (1763 BC) and Mari, uniting Mesopotamia briefly.
Palace archive on the middle Euphrates, **20,000+ tablets**, showing the shifting alliances of Hammurabi's age.

Hammurabi and Old Babylon.front: Sack of Babylon by Mursili I
Hammurabi and Old Babylon.back: Hittite raid, about **1595 BC** (middle chronology), ending Hammurabi's dynasty; the **Kassites** took over.

Primary source: Hammurabi's laws on eyes.back: Black stone, about **2.25 m**, about **1750s BC**, with about **282 laws**; taken to Susa as plunder; found **1901–02**; now in the **Louvre**.

Primary source: Hammurabi's laws on eyes.front: Why does the same injury cost differently in laws 196–199?
Primary source: Hammurabi's laws on eyes.back: The penalty depends on **rank**: a free man gets **talion** (eye for eye), a commoner (*muškēnum*) gets **silver**, a slave's owner gets **half the slave's value**.
Copied for a thousand years and matches practice, **but court records almost never cite it**; many read it as a **royal monument of justice** as much as a code.

Kerma: the kingdom of Kush that rivalled.back: Capital of **Kush** above the Nile's **Third Cataract** (Sudan); peak about **1750–1500 BC**; the **Western Deffufa** temple.
Title of the **Egyptian viceroy** who ruled Nubia after **Thutmose I destroyed Kerma** about 1500 BC.

Kerma: the kingdom of Kush that rivalled.front: How did Kush threaten Egypt about 1600 BC?
Kerma: the kingdom of Kush that rivalled.back: Its armies **raided deep into Egypt** (Elkab inscription), and the Hyksos king wrote to Kush proposing to **divide Egypt** between them (Kamose's stela).

The Hyksos: foreign kings in the Nile De.back: From *heqau khasut*, **"rulers of foreign lands"**: West Semitic 15th Dynasty at **Avaris**, about **1650–1550 BC**.
Manetho (200s BC) says **invasion**; Avaris archaeology and **strontium isotopes** (2020) show **long-term immigration** before and during their rule. Most now lean gradual.
Theban king who **took Avaris** about **1550 BC**, expelled the Hyksos and founded the **New Kingdom**.

The Hittites of Hattusa.back: Hittite capital near **Boğazkale**, central Anatolia; its archive found from **1906**; abandoned about **1185–1180 BC**.
Czech scholar who showed in **1915** that Hittite is **Indo-European**, the oldest written member of the family.
Hittite king, about **1350–1322 BC**; **destroyed Mitanni** and took Syria.

The Hittites of Hattusa.front: Did the Hittites have a secret of iron?
The Hittites of Hattusa.back: **No.** They worked some iron, but it was rare and costly everywhere; iron became common only **after the collapse**.

Mitanni, the Kassites and the rise of As.back: Hurrian kingdom of northern Syria and Mesopotamia, about **1550–1300 BC**, with **Indo-Aryan-named kings**.

Mitanni, the Kassites and the rise of As.front: Why does Mitanni matter for Indian history?
Mitanni, the Kassites and the rise of As.back: Its treaty of about **1350 BC** swears by **Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas**, Rigvedic gods: Indo-Aryan speakers were in **Syria by about 1400 BC**.
Rulers of **Babylon** about **1595–1155 BC**, the longest dynasty in its history; ended by an **Elamite raid** that took Hammurabi's stele.
Assyrian king, about **1363–1328 BC**; threw off Mitanni and wrote to Egypt as a **great king**: the start of Middle Assyria.

Egypt's New Kingdom builds an empire.back: About **1457 BC**: **Thutmose III** beats a Canaanite coalition after a march through a narrow pass; the first battle recorded in detail.
About **1479–1425 BC**; some **17 campaigns** in the Levant; Annals carved at **Karnak**.

Egypt's New Kingdom builds an empire.front: How did Egypt rule the Levant, and how Nubia?
Egypt's New Kingdom builds an empire.back: The **Levant** through local **vassal kings** who sent tribute and sons; **Nubia** was **annexed** and ruled by a viceroy for its gold.

Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled as king.back: Daughter of Thutmose I; regent for Thutmose III, then **king about 1473–1458 BC**; temple at **Deir el-Bahari**; expedition to **Punt**.
About **20 years after her death**, so probably **succession politics** (a clean line from Thutmose I to III and his son), not personal revenge. Unproven either way.

Akhenaten, the Aten and the city of Amar.back: Pharaoh about **1352–1336 BC**; raised the **Aten** (sun disc) above all gods and founded **Akhetaten (Amarna)** about 1346 BC.
For: one god, other cults suppressed. Against: the Aten was reached only **through the royal family**, households kept old gods, and it also **took power from Amun's priests**. Many hold both.
Boy-king after Akhenaten who **restored Amun** and left Amarna; famous because **Howard Carter found his tomb intact, 1922**.

The Amarna letters and the club of great.back: About **380 cuneiform tablets**, about **1360–1330 BC**, found **1887**: the pharaohs' foreign mail, mostly in **Akkadian**.

The Amarna letters and the club of great.front: How did the Bronze Age great powers deal with each other?
The Amarna letters and the club of great.back: As **"brothers"**: gift exchange (Egyptian gold for horses, lapis, copper), **royal marriages**, envoys and letters in Akkadian, the shared diplomatic language.
Off south Turkey, about **1300 BC**: about **10 tonnes of copper and 1 tonne of tin**, plus goods from many cultures.
Uprooted bands outside city control, complained of in the vassal letters; **a social class, not one people**.

Ramesses II, Kadesh and the treaty with.back: **1274 BC**, on the Orontes in Syria: **Ramesses II v. Muwatalli II**; a great chariot battle, claimed as a victory by Ramesses.
Tactically **a draw Ramesses survived**; strategically **a Hittite gain**: Kadesh stayed Hittite. Ramesses' temple accounts are **propaganda**.
About **1259 BC**, Ramesses II and **Hattusili III**: peace, mutual defence, extradition; **both versions survive**.

Minoan Crete and the eruption of Thera.back: Largest Minoan palace on Crete, from about **1950 BC**; excavated by **Arthur Evans** from **1900**.
Minoan script for accounts, **still undeciphered**; not apparently Greek.
**Radiocarbon** says about **1600 BC**; the **archaeological** sequence tied to Egypt says about **1500 BC**. Unsettled; a tree-ring or ice-core signal would decide.

Mycenaean Greece, Linear B and the quest.back: Mycenaean script, deciphered by **Michael Ventris in 1952** as **early Greek**; palace accounts baked by fire.
Kingdom west of the Hittites in their texts; most scholars identify it with **Mycenaean Greeks** (Homer's Achaeans).
Plausible: Troy (**Hisarlik**) was rich and burned about 1300–1180 BC; Hittites record trouble at **Wilusa**. But no text names Greek attackers, and Homer wrote about **750–700 BC**.

Bronze Age Europe: tin, amber and the Ne.back: Bronze and gold disc showing **sun or moon, crescent and stars (Pleiades?)**, Germany, about **1600 BC**; found by looters 1999. A 2020 Iron Age redating is a minority view.
North-east Germany, about **1250 BC**: bones of **well over 100 people**; Europe's oldest large-scale battlefield.

Bronze Age Europe: tin, amber and the Ne.front: Why did the Mediterranean kingdoms need Europe?
Bronze Age Europe: tin, amber and the Ne.back: For **tin** (Cornwall, Brittany, Iberia, Ore Mountains) to make bronze, and **Baltic amber** as a luxury.

Ugarit and the invention of the alphabet.back: Earliest alphabet, about **1900–1500 BC**, by Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt's orbit (Serabit el-Khadim, Wadi el-Hol).

Ugarit and the invention of the alphabet.front: How did the first alphabet work?
Ugarit and the invention of the alphabet.back: By **acrophony**: an Egyptian picture stood for the **first sound of its name** in Semitic: *ʾalp* (ox) for ʾ, *bayt* (house) for b. Consonants only.
Port at **Ras Shamra**, Syria; a **30-letter cuneiform alphabet** (1300s–1200s BC) and the Baal myths; destroyed about **1185 BC**.

The fading of the Indus cities, about 19.back: About **1900–1300 BC**: Indus cities empty, the script, seals and weights end, settlement shifts **east and south**: **de-urbanisation**.

The fading of the Indus cities, about 19.front: Why did the Indus cities decline?
The fading of the Indus cities, about 19.back: Probably **several causes**: a **weaker monsoon** (4.2-kiloyear event), **shifting rivers** (Ghaggar-Hakra), and **lost Gulf trade**. Debated.
**No.** Wheeler's 1940s claim fell when **George Dales (1964)** showed the 'massacre' skeletons came from different periods.

The Vedic peoples and the Rigveda.back: **1,028 hymns** in Vedic Sanskrit, composed roughly **1500–1200 BC** in the **Punjab**; preserved **orally** for over a thousand years.
Rigvedic battle won by the **Bharata** tribe on the **Ravi** river.

The Vedic peoples and the Rigveda.front: How did Indo-Aryan reach India? The two readings
The Vedic peoples and the Rigveda.back: **Migration** (most linguists, geneticists): steppe ancestry arrives **2000–1500 BC**, Indo-Aryan in Mitanni about 1400 BC. **Indigenous**: no intrusive culture, Harappan continuity, no memory of migration. Both reject a violent 'invasion'.

The Shang dynasty and the bronze of Anya.back: Last **Shang capital**, about **1250–1046 BC**, from King **Wu Ding**; palaces, royal tombs, oracle bones.
Consort of Wu Ding who **led armies**; her unrobbed tomb, found **1976**, held hundreds of bronzes and jades.
Sichuan bronze culture, about **1200–1000 BC**: giant bronze masks; proof China had **several centres**.
About **1046 BC**: **King Wu of Zhou** defeats the last Shang king.

Oracle bones: China's first writing.back: Drill hollows in an **ox scapula or turtle plastron**, apply heat until it **cracks**, the **king reads** the crack, the question and outcome are **carved** beside it.
Scholar who showed in **1917** that oracle bones confirm **Sima Qian's list of Shang kings**.
About **1250–1046 BC**; about **4,000** characters known; the direct ancestor of **Chinese writing today**.

The Olmec, and the Americas around 1200.back: First great **Olmec** centre, Gulf Coast of Mexico, peak about **1200–900 BC**; colossal basalt heads.
Louisiana, about **1700–1100 BC**: huge concentric earth ridges and mounds built by **hunter-fisher-gatherers**.

The Olmec, and the Americas around 1200.front: Olmec: mother culture or sister cultures?
The Olmec, and the Americas around 1200.back: **Mother**: Olmec motifs earliest and best at San Lorenzo, which exported pottery. **Sister**: several regions developed together and **shared** symbols by exchange. Unsettled.

The Lapita voyagers of the Pacific.back: Austronesian voyagers with **dentate-stamped pottery**, from the Bismarcks about **1350–1300 BC** to **Samoa about 800 BC**.
Cemetery in **Vanuatu**, about 1000 BC; its ancient DNA (2016) showed the first settlers had **almost entirely East Asian ancestry**.

The Lapita voyagers of the Pacific.front: How did Lapita sailors cross 850 km of open sea safely?
The Lapita voyagers of the Pacific.back: In **outrigger or double canoes**, sailing **against the prevailing wind**, so they could run home downwind if they found nothing; carrying pigs, dogs, chickens, taro and yams.

The Late Bronze Age collapse and the Sea.back: Temple of **Ramesses III** showing his defeat of the **Sea Peoples**, about **1177 BC**: Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh.
About **1208 BC**; records victory over Libyans and northern peoples, and the **first mention of Israel** outside the Bible.
One of the Sea Peoples, settled on the coast of Canaan: the **Philistines**.

The Late Bronze Age collapse and the Sea.front: Why did the Bronze Age collapse? The main readings
The Late Bronze Age collapse and the Sea.back: **Invaders**, **drought**, **earthquakes**, **revolt**, **new infantry warfare**, or a **systems collapse** of an interdependent world (Cline). Most lean to **several causes together**, often with drought central.

Connections: the world around 1000 BC.front: What carried from the Bronze Age into the next age?
Connections: the world around 1000 BC.back: **Iron**, the **alphabet**, Hammurabi's model of the **just king**, **Assyria's** ambition, the **Mandate of Heaven** and the **Vedas**.
Chinese dynasty from about **1046 BC**, ruling by the **Mandate of Heaven**.

Connections: the world around 1000 BC.front: How did gods travel in the Bronze Age?
Connections: the world around 1000 BC.back: With **kings and peoples**, not missionaries: Amun to **Nubia**, Mesopotamian myths to the **Hittites**, Vedic gods to **Mitanni and India**.

Map: the world in 800 BC.front: Why did iron spread further than bronze?
Map: the world in 800 BC.back: Iron ore is **common**; tin and copper are not. Once smelting was mastered, **many more people** could have iron tools and weapons.

Map: the world in 800 BC.front: Lapita reach Fiji, Tonga and Samoa
Map: the world in 800 BC.back: About **900–800 BC**: the edge of the inhabited Pacific for **centuries** afterwards.
The **common language** of the Near East in this age, written in an alphabet from Phoenician; the chancery language of **Persia**.

The axial age: Jaspers's idea and its cr.back: German philosopher, **1949**: between about **800 and 200 BC** thinkers in China, India, Iran, Israel and Greece turned history on an axis.

The axial age: Jaspers's idea and its cr.front: The strongest objections to the axial age
The axial age: Jaspers's idea and its cr.back: **Dates stretched** (Zarathustra may be far earlier); **earlier societies** had moral gods too; the **Seshat** data (2018) do not cluster; it **leaves out** Africa and the Americas.

The axial age: Jaspers's idea and its cr.front: Baumard's explanation of the axial age (2015)
The axial age: Jaspers's idea and its cr.back: **Rising affluence**: once enough people lived above subsistence, ascetic and moral teachings appealed.

The Neo-Assyrian empire: Nineveh and the.back: Assyrian king **745–727 BC**: standing army, **provinces under governors**, mass deportation — raiding turned into ruling.
**612 BC**, to **Babylon** (Nabopolassar) and the **Medes** (Cyaxares). Assyria's last stand at Harran ended **609**.
Nineveh, 7th century BC: tens of thousands of tablets, including the ***Epic of Gilgamesh***; now mostly in the **British Museum**.

The Neo-Assyrian empire: Nineveh and the.front: Why did Assyria advertise its cruelty?
The Neo-Assyrian empire: Nineveh and the.back: Palace reliefs of flaying and impalement were **shown to envoys**: terror made **surrender cheaper than resistance**.

The Phoenicians: Tyre, purple and the al.back: Dye from the **murex** sea snail; thousands of snails for a few grams — the colour of **kings**.

The Phoenicians: Tyre, purple and the al.front: Why does most of the world's writing descend from Phoenician?
The Phoenicians: Tyre, purple and the al.back: Its **22-letter alphabet** (by about 1050 BC) was borrowed by the **Greeks** (about 800 BC, adding vowels) and the **Aramaeans**, ancestors of Latin, Hebrew, Arabic and Indian scripts.
About **600 BC**, told by **Herodotus**: Phoenicians said the sun was **on their right** going west. Possible; **unproven**.

Israel and Judah: two kingdoms between t.back: Moabite inscription, about **840 BC**: Mesha throws off the rule of **Omri, king of Israel**.
Aramaean inscription, **9th century BC**: most read **"House of David"** — David's dynasty outside the Bible.
**722–720 BC**, to **Assyria**: the northern kingdom of Israel ends; its people partly deported.

Israel and Judah: two kingdoms between t.front: Maximalists, minimalists and the middle ground
Israel and Judah: two kingdoms between t.back: **Maximalists**: the Bible broadly reliable from David. **Minimalists**: late texts, David a chief at most. **Finkelstein**: real dynasty, small 10th-century Judah. Agreed: **reliable from about 850 BC**.

Kush: the 25th dynasty and Napata.back: King of **Kush**, about 744–714 BC; conquered Egypt about **728 BC**; his **victory stela** at Jebel Barkal.
25th-dynasty pharaoh, **690–664 BC**; great builder; largest pyramid at **Nuri**; fought **Assyria**.

Kush: the 25th dynasty and Napata.front: How did Kushite rule in Egypt end?
Kush: the 25th dynasty and Napata.back: **Assyria**: Esarhaddon took **Memphis (671)**, Ashurbanipal sacked **Thebes (663)**; Kush withdrew south.

Zhou China: the Mandate of Heaven and th.back: Zhou idea: Heaven gives rule to the **virtuous** and **withdraws it** from the wicked. Claimed by every later dynasty.
King You killed; the Zhou court moves east to **Luoyi** — the start of the **Eastern Zhou**.
**770–476 BC**, named after the annals of **Lu**: royal power gone, states led by **hegemons**.

The Greek polis: colonies, hoplites and.back: Greek **city-state**: town, farmland, laws, gods, army. **Over a thousand** of them.
**733 BC**, by **Corinth**, in Sicily — one of the colonies of about 750–550 BC.
Citizen spearman in bronze armour with a round shield, in the **phalanx**, from the **7th century BC**.

The Greek polis: colonies, hoplites and.front: Was a Greek tyrant a bad ruler?
The Greek polis: colonies, hoplites and.back: Not necessarily: a **tyrant** seized power **outside the law**, often with popular support. **Pisistratus** of Athens built temples and fountains.

The Etruscans.back: Modern **Tuscany** and northern Lazio; a league of about **twelve cities**; height about **650–500 BC**.

The Etruscans.front: Etruscan origins: what does ancient DNA say?
The Etruscans.back: A **2021** study found them genetically like their **Latin neighbours**: **local origin**, against Herodotus's migration from Lydia.
About **500 BC**: gold sheets in **Etruscan and Phoenician**, a key to the partly understood language.

The Scythians: horse archers of the step.back: Royal mound in **Tuva**, Siberia, about **800 BC**: the earliest great 'Scythian' burial — origins in the **east**.
About **513 BC**: the Scythians retreated and **refused battle**; Darius withdrew.
Frozen tombs in the **Altai**, about 4th–3rd centuries BC: felt, carpets, tattooed bodies, **hemp braziers** confirming Herodotus.

The Celts: Hallstatt and La Tène.back: Upper **Austria**, **salt mines**; the Iron Age culture of about **800–450 BC**.
Site on Lake **Neuchâtel**, Switzerland; Celtic art style **from about 450 BC** — swirls, spirals, torcs.
Burgundy, about **500 BC**: Greek bronze bowl **1.64 m** tall in a woman's grave.
Simon **James**, John **Collis**: no ancient writer called Britons 'Celts'; **language, art and identity** did not travel together.

The Olmec, Monte Albán and the early May.back: Olmec centre in **Tabasco**, about **900–400 BC**; clay pyramid about **30 m** high.
**Mother**: the Olmec invented Mesoamerica's core and spread it. **Sister**: many regions developed together. Turns on **which region shows each symbol first**.
Zapotec hilltop city in **Oaxaca**, founded about **500 BC**; the **Danzantes** carvings.
Maya platform about **1.4 km** long, about **1000–800 BC**, found by **lidar** in 2020.

Chavín de Huántar and the Andes.back: Temple at about **3,150 m** in the Peruvian Andes, roughly **1200/900–500/200 BC** (dating debated).
Granite blade about **4.5 m** tall, a fanged being, in the dark galleries of Chavín's **Old Temple**.

Chavín de Huántar and the Andes.front: How did Chavín's influence spread without an army?
Chavín de Huántar and the Andes.back: By **pilgrimage, trade and imitation**: a religious centre, not an empire — the **Early Horizon**.

Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, 626–539 BC.back: King of Babylon **605–562 BC**; won at **Carchemish** (605); took **Jerusalem** (597, 587/586); built the **Ishtar Gate**.

Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, 626–539 BC.front: Were the Hanging Gardens at Babylon?
Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, 626–539 BC.back: **No Babylonian text** mentions them. **Dalley** (2013): at **Nineveh**, by Sennacherib. Others: lost at Babylon, or legend.
Babylonian sky records from about **652 BC** to the 1st century BC — the longest **scientific record** of antiquity.
**October 539 BC**: after **Opis**, Babylon taken **without a battle**; Nabonidus the last king.

Exile and return: Judah under Babylon an.back: 'Judah-town' in Babylonia, about **572–477 BC**: exiles as **tenant farmers**, not slaves.
**515 BC**, in Darius I's sixth year.
Jewish garrison on the **Nile** in Persian service, with its own temple; petition of **407 BC**.

Cyrus the Great builds the Persian empir.back: King of **Anshan** (Fars) from about **559 BC**; took Media (**550**), Lydia (**547–546**), Babylon (**539**); died **530**.
**Policy real**: return of gods and peoples. **Label rejected** by most: a standard **Mesopotamian royal inscription** legitimising a conqueror.
Cyrus's capital in **Fars**, where his stone **tomb** still stands.

Darius I: satrapies, the Royal Road and.back: Darius I's cliff text, after **522 BC**, in **Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian** — the key to **deciphering cuneiform**.
Persian **provincial governor**; Herodotus lists **twenty** tax districts.
About **2,500 km**, **Sardis to Susa**, with 111 stations; relay couriers covered it in about a **week**.

Darius I: satrapies, the Royal Road and.front: Did Darius kill an impostor or the real Bardiya?
Darius I: satrapies, the Royal Road and.back: **Open**: Darius's own account is the main source; many suspect he **covered a usurpation**.

Zoroastrianism as history.back: Seventeen hymns in **Old Avestan**, thought to be **Zarathustra's own words**.
**Early** (about 1500–1000 BC, Boyce): Gathas' language near the Rigveda. **Late** (6th century BC): '258 years before Alexander'. **Unsettled**.
Zoroastrians who moved from Iran to **India** from about the **8th–10th centuries AD**.

India's mahajanapadas and the rise of Ma.back: The **sixteen** 'great realms' of north India, about **600 BC** onwards, listed in Buddhist texts.
Indian **'republic'**: rule by an assembly of clan heads, e.g. the **Vajji** league at Vaishali.
Rich farmland, **iron ore**, **elephants** and the **Ganges** for transport.
Magadha's capital on the Ganges, modern **Patna**.

The Buddha and Mahavira: the shramana mo.back: Wandering **ascetic** ('striver') of the Ganges valley who questioned **Vedic sacrifice**.
**Long chronology**: about 483 BC. **Short**: about 400–370 BC; many specialists lean to **about 400 BC**.
Vardhamana, born near **Vaishali**; Jainism's **24th Tirthankara**; older contemporary of the Buddha.
Deer park near **Varanasi**: the Buddha's **first sermon**.

Confucius and the Hundred Schools.back: **551–479 BC** (traditional), state of **Lu** (Shandong); his sayings in the ***Analects***.
About **470–391 BC**: **impartial care** for all; against offensive war.
Human nature is **good**; a tyrant has **lost the Mandate**, and may rightfully be overthrown.

Sparta: helots, the agoge and the Sparta.back: State-owned **serfs** of Laconia and **Messenia**, who greatly **outnumbered** the Spartans.
Spartan state upbringing of boys from **age seven**.
**371 BC**: **Thebes** crushes Sparta, then frees Messenia.
Ollier, **1933**: almost all we know is by **outsiders** who idealised or used Sparta; archaeology shows Archaic Sparta **richer** than the legend.

Athens invents democracy: Solon to Ephia.back: Athenian archon, **594 BC**: cancelled debts, **banned debt slavery**, classes by **wealth**.
**508/7 BC**: ten tribes, demes, **Council of 500** by lot — the founding of democracy.
Vote on potsherds to **exile a man for ten years**; first used **487 BC**.

Athens invents democracy: Solon to Ephia.front: Why did Athens choose officials by lot?
Athens invents democracy: Solon to Ephia.back: Athenians thought **elections favoured the rich and famous**; lot was the democratic method.

Carthage: from Tyrian colony to western.back: By **Tyre**, traditionally **814 BC** (archaeology late 9th–8th century); 'new city', in **Tunisia**.
**480 BC**: Gelon of Syracuse destroys a Carthaginian army in Sicily.
Carthage's **two annual chief magistrates**; Aristotle praised its constitution.
Urns of burnt **infants**: **child sacrifice** (ancient writers, vow inscriptions) or **children's cemetery** (2010 bone study)? Most lean to **some sacrifice**; not closed.

The Persian Wars, 499–479 BC.back: **490 BC**: Athenians and Plataeans under **Miltiades** defeat Darius's force.
**August 480 BC**: **Leonidas**, 300 Spartans and allies hold the pass three days.
**September 480 BC**: the Greek fleet, Athenian at its heart, wrecks Xerxes' navy.

The Persian Wars, 499–479 BC.front: Why do historians reject Herodotus's figure for Xerxes' army?
The Persian Wars, 499–479 BC.back: He gives **1.7 million** fighting men; Greece **could not have fed them**. Modern estimates: **low hundreds of thousands at most**.

Athens' fifth-century empire and the age.back: **478/7 BC**, Athens-led alliance against Persia; treasury moved to **Athens in 454** — league became empire.
Temple of Athena, **447–432 BC**, under **Phidias**, paid partly from league money.

Athens' fifth-century empire and the age.front: Did the allies hate the Athenian empire?
Athens' fifth-century empire and the age.back: **Thucydides**: a hated tyranny. **De Ste. Croix**: the **common people** often favoured Athens, which backed democrats; hatred mainly among the **rich**.

Primary source: Pericles' Funeral Oratio.front: Is the Funeral Oration Pericles' own words?
Primary source: Pericles' Funeral Oratio.back: **Thucydides' version**: by his own account (1.22) he wrote what speakers should have said, **keeping the general sense**.

Primary source: Pericles' Funeral Oratio.front: Why does the plague follow the Funeral Oration?
Primary source: Pericles' Funeral Oratio.back: Thucydides sets **the ideal beside its collapse**: the plague of **430 BC** comes in the next chapters.

The Peloponnesian War, 431–404 BC.back: **The growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta.** Kagan: avoidable; de Ste. Croix: **Sparta and Corinth** the aggressors.
**415–413 BC**: Athens' attack on **Syracuse**; the whole force destroyed.
**405 BC**: **Lysander** destroys the Athenian fleet; Athens surrenders **404**.
**416 BC**: Athens kills the men and enslaves the rest; Thucydides' **Melian Dialogue**.

Laozi, Shang Yang and the Warring States.back: **475–221 BC** (start dates vary): seven states, mass infantry, iron, **crossbow**.
Reformer of **Qin**, about **356–338 BC**: group responsibility, **rank by merit in war**, harsh public law.
Bamboo texts from a tomb sealed about **300 BC**: the **oldest copy** of parts of the *Daodejing*.
**Legalists**: people respond to **reward and punishment**, so rule by clear law. **Confucius**: rule by **virtue and ritual**.

Early Rome: from kings to the conquest o.back: Traditionally **509 BC**: the last king expelled; **two annual consuls**.

Early Rome: from kings to the conquest o.front: How did Rome grow after the Latin War (338 BC)?
Early Rome: from kings to the conquest o.back: By **adding manpower**: citizenship or partial rights for Latins, and allies who **supplied soldiers**.

Early Rome: from kings to the conquest o.front: How reliable is early Roman history?
Early Rome: from kings to the conquest o.back: Livy wrote after **30 BC**; records lost in the Gallic sack. **Optimists** (Cornell): outline sound. **Sceptics**: much reconstructed. Sequence accepted, **stories and dates not**.

Meroë, Nok and Africa's iron age.back: Kushite city on the Nile in Sudan, with **rain, iron ore and wood**; the royal cemetery moved there about **300 BC**.
Central **Nigeria**, about **1500 BC**–turn of the era; **terracotta** heads from about **900 BC**; iron by mid-millennium.

Meroë, Nok and Africa's iron age.front: Did African iron-working spread from outside or arise there?
Meroë, Nok and Africa's iron age.back: **Diffusion** (from Carthage or the Nile) or **independent invention** (early dates, different furnaces). Hard to settle: **radiocarbon** for the period is imprecise.
Kingdom in **Eritrea and northern Ethiopia**, about 8th–5th centuries BC; temple at **Yeha** in the style of Saba.

Philip II and Alexander the Great.back: Macedonian pike about **5–6 m** long, Philip II's phalanx weapon.
**338 BC**: Philip II crushes **Athens and Thebes**.
**331 BC**: Alexander breaks the army of **Darius III**.

Connections: the world in 300 BC.back: **Lydia**, western Anatolia, late **7th century BC**; separately in **China** and **India**.

Connections: the world in 300 BC.front: Did the new ideas of the axial age spread abroad before 300 BC?
Connections: the world in 300 BC.back: **Very little yet**: Buddhism, Confucianism, Zoroastrianism stayed at home; the exception, the **Jewish diaspora**.
Silk and a mirror in **Altai** tombs, 4th–3rd centuries BC: goods crossing Asia **before the Silk Road**.

Map: the world in 300 BC.back: Founder of the **Mauryan empire**, about **321 BC**, ruling northern India from **Pataliputra**.
Seafarers reached **Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BC**; eastern Polynesia was still empty in this stage.

Map: the world in 300 BC.front: Why compare Rome and Han China?
Map: the world in 300 BC.back: Two empires at the same time, each ruling perhaps **50–60 million** people, roughly a quarter of humanity apiece, and linked by trade though never by travel.

Alexander's heirs: the wars of the Succe.back: The **Successors**: Alexander's generals, who fought over his empire after his death in **323 BC**.
**301 BC**, Anatolia: the Successors' coalition killed **Antigonus the One-Eyed**, ending any hope of one Hellenistic empire.
The **common Greek** of the Hellenistic world, from Sicily to the Indus; the language of the New Testament.
**Ptolemies** in Egypt (to 30 BC), **Seleucids** in Syria–Iran (to 63 BC), **Antigonids** in Macedon (to 168 BC).

Ptolemaic Egypt and the Library of Alexa.back: **196 BC** decree for Ptolemy V in **hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek**; key to Champollion's decipherment, **1822**.
Alexandrian scholar who measured **the Earth's circumference** from shadow angles, about **240 BC**.

Ptolemaic Egypt and the Library of Alexa.front: How did the Library of Alexandria end?
Ptolemaic Egypt and the Library of Alexa.back: **Disputed**: Caesar's fire (48 BC), wars of the 270s, the Serapeum's destruction (391), slow loss of funding. The Arab burning of 642 is **probably legend**.

The Seleucids, Bactria and the Greek Eas.back: **Greek city** on the Oxus in northern **Afghanistan**, with gymnasium, theatre and Delphic maxims; excavated from 1965.
**190 BC**: Rome defeated **Antiochus III**; the Treaty of Apamea (188) took most of Asia Minor from the Seleucids.
Jewish rising against **Antiochus IV** from **167 BC**; Temple rededicated **164 BC** (Hanukkah); the Hasmonean kingdom followed.

Rome's rise in Italy, 509–264 BC.back: Officer of the common people who could **veto** any act of the Roman state.
From **Pyrrhus of Epirus**, who beat Rome at Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279) at **ruinous cost**.

Rome's rise in Italy, 509–264 BC.front: Why did Rome's conquest of Italy feed further conquest?
Rome's rise in Italy, 509–264 BC.back: Defeated peoples became **allies who had to send soldiers**, so each victory **enlarged Rome's manpower**.

Carthage and the First Punic War.back: Phoenician city near **Tunis**, traditionally founded **814 BC** from Tyre; the western Mediterranean's great sea power.
Roman **boarding bridge** with a spike, used to turn sea battles into land fights; first won at **Mylae, 260 BC**.

Carthage and the First Punic War.front: Why did Sicily matter after 241 BC?
Carthage and the First Punic War.back: It became Rome's **first province**: governed by a Roman official and **taxed**, unlike the Italian allies.

Hannibal and the Second Punic War.back: **216 BC**, Apulia: Hannibal's **double envelopment** destroyed a larger Roman army; tens of thousands killed.
"**The Delayer**": shadowed Hannibal and **avoided battle**, starving him of supplies.
**202 BC**: **Scipio Africanus** defeated Hannibal in Africa, ending the Second Punic War.

Hannibal and the Second Punic War.front: Why didn't Rome fall after Cannae?
Hannibal and the Second Punic War.back: **Central Italy's allies stayed loyal**, Rome refused to negotiate, and Hannibal could never take Rome itself.

Rome masters the Mediterranean, 200–133.back: The year Rome destroyed both **Carthage** and **Corinth**; Africa and Macedonia became provinces.
Greek hostage in Rome (from **167 BC**) who wrote a history to explain **how Rome conquered the world** so fast.
Large Roman **estates worked by slave gangs**, spreading as conquest brought wealth and captives.

The Gracchi, Marius and Sulla: the Repub.back: Tribune in **133 BC**; proposed sharing public land among the poor; **killed by senators**.
**91–88 BC**: Rome's Italian allies revolted; Rome won but granted them **citizenship**.
**88 BC**: the first Roman to **lead his army against the city**; later dictator (82–79) with proscriptions.
Marius enlisted propertyless volunteers (**107 BC**), but many historians see the professional army as a **gradual change**, not one reform.

Caesar crosses the Rubicon.back: River marking Caesar's province; crossing it in **January 49 BC** meant **civil war**.
**52 BC**: Caesar besieged and defeated **Vercingetorix**, ending Gallic resistance.
**15 March 44 BC**: Caesar stabbed by senators led by **Brutus and Cassius**.

Caesar crosses the Rubicon.front: Why did the Republic fall: Syme v. Gruen
Caesar crosses the Rubicon.back: **Syme**: a city-state could not run an empire, so one-man rule was near-inevitable. **Gruen**: the Republic still worked; **the war of 49** destroyed it.

Augustus and the making of the principat.back: **31 BC**, off western Greece: Octavian's fleet under Agrippa beat **Antony and Cleopatra**.
"**First citizen**": Augustus's title, so his system is called the **principate** (from **27 BC**).
**AD 9**: **Arminius** destroyed three legions under Varus; the **Rhine** became Rome's frontier.
Augustus's own **record of his achievements**; best copy on a temple in **Ankara**.

The Pax Romana, from Tiberius to Marcus.back: Emperor **98–117**, born in Spain; conquered **Dacia**; empire at its **largest** at his death.
Begun about **122** across northern Britain; **80 Roman miles** of stone with forts.
Epidemic from about **165**, probably **smallpox**; its death toll is **strongly debated**.
**212**: Caracalla gave **citizenship to almost all free people** in the empire.

Running an empire: provinces, roads and.front: How did Rome govern so many with so few officials?
Running an empire: provinces, roads and.back: Through **self-governing cities**: local councils (**decuriones**) collected taxes, kept order and paid for buildings.
The Roman **imperial post** along the road network, for official messengers.
**Imposed** by Roman policy (as Tacitus describes), or **chosen and mixed** by provincials themselves; household archaeology shows great variety.

Primary source: Tacitus on Roman Britain.back: Tacitus's life of his father-in-law, **governor of Britain about 77–84**, written about **AD 98**.
Caledonian chief to whom Tacitus gives the speech before **Mons Graupius** (83 or 84): **"they make a solitude and call it peace"**.

Primary source: Tacitus on Roman Britain.front: Why not take Calgacus's speech as his own words?
Primary source: Tacitus on Roman Britain.back: Ancient historians **composed speeches** for their characters; Tacitus was **not there** and wrote 14 years later.

Judea under Rome and the Jewish revolts,.back: Jewish general who went over to Rome and wrote the ***Jewish War***; our main source for the revolt of **66–73/74**.
**AD 70**, by **Titus**; shown on the **Arch of Titus** in Rome.
**132–135/136** under Hadrian; afterwards Jews were **banned from Jerusalem**, renamed Aelia Capitolina.
First great written collection of **rabbinic law**, about **200**, by **Judah ha-Nasi**.

Christianity's first three centuries.back: Greek-speaking Jewish follower whose **letters (50s)** are the earliest Christian writings; opened the movement to **Gentiles**.
**250**: **everyone** ordered to sacrifice and get a certificate; the first empire-wide persecution.
Began **303** under **Diocletian**; lasted in the East until **311–313**.

Christianity's first three centuries.front: How did Trajan tell Pliny to treat Christians (about 112)?
Christianity's first three centuries.back: **Do not hunt them**; punish those **accused** who refuse to sacrifice.

The third-century crisis, 235–284.back: **260**: the emperor taken prisoner by **Shapur I** of Persia near Edessa; died in captivity.
Queen of **Palmyra** who took Egypt and much of the East (**270–272**) until Aurelian defeated her.
Emperor **270–275**; reunited the empire (**274**) and built new **walls round Rome**.

The third-century crisis, 235–284.front: Why did emperors fall so fast in 235–284?
The third-century crisis, 235–284.back: Any general facing a threat **where the emperor wasn't** could be proclaimed by his troops; each usurpation weakened the frontier.

Diocletian and the tetrarchy.back: "**Rule of four**": two senior emperors (Augusti) and two juniors (Caesars), from **293**.
**301**: ceiling prices on over a thousand goods and wages; it **failed**, but records ancient prices.
Not the succession plan, which failed within years, but the **administrative state**: small provinces, big army, regular tax, court ceremony.

Parthia, Rome's rival beyond the Euphrat.back: Parthia's dynasty, from **Arsaces I** (about **247 BC**) to **AD 224**.
**53 BC**: **Crassus** killed and his army destroyed by Surena's horse archers.
Han envoy sent by Ban Chao in **AD 97** to reach Rome; turned back at a great sea.
We see it mostly **through Roman eyes**, plus coins; the Sasanians who replaced it had reason to belittle it.

The Sasanians take Iran.back: From **Persis**; killed the last Parthian king at Hormozdgan in **224**; "King of Kings of Iran".

The Sasanians take Iran.front: Naqsh-e Rostam inscription of Shapur I
The Sasanians take Iran.back: Shapur's trilingual record (**Middle Persian, Parthian, Greek**) of his victories over Rome.
Prophet (**216–274/277**) who founded **Manichaeism**; died in prison under Bahram I.

The Mauryas: Chandragupta and Ashoka.back: About **261 BC**: Ashoka's conquest of the east coast (Odisha), which he says he **regretted**.
Ashoka's moral code: respect, kindness to servants and animals, **tolerance of all sects**.
Deciphered the **Brahmi** script of Ashoka's edicts in **1837**.

The Mauryas: Chandragupta and Ashoka.front: Why is the Arthashastra's evidence for the Mauryas doubtful?
The Mauryas: Chandragupta and Ashoka.back: Though credited to Kautilya, the text as we have it was probably **compiled centuries later**.

The Kushans, the Indo-Greeks and the nor.back: Greatest **Kushan** king; accession most often dated about **AD 127**, though debated.
**Bactrian** text of Kanishka, found in Afghanistan in **1993**.
At **Vidisha**, about **110 BC**: a Greek ambassador honours the Hindu god **Vasudeva**.

The Kushans, the Indo-Greeks and the nor.front: Gandhara or Mathura: who made the first Buddha image?
The Kushans, the Indo-Greeks and the nor.back: **Disputed**: both appear around the 1st–2nd century AD under the Kushans; few sculptures are firmly dated.

The Satavahanas, the Tamil kingdoms and.back: Greatest **Satavahana** king (early **2nd century AD**); his victories recorded by his mother at **Nashik**.
About **AD 150**: early **Sanskrit** inscription recording repair of a dam first built under the Mauryas.
The three **Tamil kingdoms** of the south, known from **Sangam** poetry and Ashoka's edicts.
First great **Gupta** king, from about **319–320**; married the Licchavi princess **Kumaradevi**.

Qin Shi Huang unifies China.back: **Qin** conquered the last Warring State (Qi); **Ying Zheng** became the **First Emperor**.
Qin **legal texts** found in **1975**: a harsh but **systematic** bureaucracy.
About **8,000** clay soldiers by the First Emperor's tomb near Xi'an, found in **1974**.
**Script, coins, weights and measures, axle widths**, and government by **commanderies** under appointed officials.

The Han dynasty and Emperor Wu.back: Reigned **141–87 BC**; Confucian academy (**124 BC**), salt and iron monopolies, wars against the Xiongnu.
Court debate of **81 BC** over **state monopolies** versus light taxes and moral rule.
Recorded about **58 million** people, among the best population counts of the ancient world.
Regent who took the throne (**AD 9–23**); radical reforms, then Yellow River floods and revolt.

The Xiongnu and Zhang Qian's journey wes.back: United the **Xiongnu** from **209 BC**; surrounded the Han founder at **Baideng** (200 BC).
"**Peace through kinship**": Han princesses and yearly silk and grain sent to the Xiongnu.
Han envoy, sent about **139–138 BC** to the Yuezhi; held 10 years by the Xiongnu; back in **126 BC**.
German geographer who coined **"Silk Road"** (*Seidenstraße*) in **1877**.

Han inventions, Sima Qian and the fall o.back: Han eunuch credited with presenting **paper** in **AD 105**; older paper finds show he **improved** it.
Sima Qian's ***Records of the Grand Historian***, finished about **90s BC**: 130 chapters, model for all later official histories.
Religious rebellion of **184** under Zhang Jue; its suppression created the **warlords** who ended Han.
**Wei, Shu and Wu**, **220–280**, after Cao Pi deposed the last Han emperor.

Early Korea and Yayoi Japan.back: Han colony near **Pyongyang**, from **108 BC** to **313**; carried Chinese writing and goods.
Brought **wet-rice farming** and metals from Korea to Kyushu; start dated **300 BC** traditionally, now often **1000–800 BC**.
Queen of **Yamatai**, who sent an embassy to Wei China in **239**.
**Disputed**: northern **Kyushu** or the **Kinai** around Nara (Makimuku); Chinese directions can't be read literally.

Meroë and the rise of Aksum.back: Title of royal women of **Kush**, several ruling in their own right; the "Candace" of Acts.
Kush's writing from about the **2nd century BC**; **readable but largely not understood**.
**21–20 BC**: Augustus made peace with **Kush** on favourable terms, dropping his tribute demand.
From the late **200s**: gold, silver and bronze coins; one of very few states minting **gold**.

The Bantu expansion.back: Early **iron-age** pottery of Bantu speakers in the **Great Lakes**, by around **500 BC**.

The Bantu expansion.front: How do we know about the Bantu expansion without writing?

The Bantu expansion.back: Central **Nigeria**, about **900 BC–AD 1**; terracotta heads and early **iron-smelting**.

Teotihuacan, the early Maya and the Hope.back: City in the Basin of Mexico; peak about **AD 400–550**, perhaps **100,000+** people; true name unknown.
Huge **Preclassic Maya** city in northern Guatemala, about **300 BC–AD 100**.
Earliest dated lowland **Maya** monument: Long Count date **AD 292**.
**Ohio and Illinois** valleys, about **200 BC–AD 500**: geometric earthworks and a continent-wide **exchange network**.

The Nazca and the Moche.back: Lines, trapezoids and **animal figures** cleared on Peru's south-coast desert, about **100 BC–AD 600**.
Untouched **Moche** royal tomb, about the **3rd century AD**, excavated by **Walter Alva** in **1987**.

The Nazca and the Moche.front: What were the Nazca lines for?
The Nazca and the Moche.back: **Debated**: astronomy (Reiche; weakened by Hawkins's 1968 test), **ritual walking**, or **water and fertility**; most now favour ritual tied to water.

Connections: the Silk Roads and the Indi.back: Greek merchant's guide, **mid-1st century AD**, to ports from **Adulis** to **Muziris**.
Roman gold medallion of **Antoninus Pius** (**152**) found at a **Funan** port in the Mekong delta.
**Parthian** monk translating Buddhist texts at **Luoyang** from about **148**.

Connections: the Silk Roads and the Indi.front: How did ships cross the Indian Ocean?
Connections: the Silk Roads and the Indi.back: By the **monsoon**: south-west winds out in summer, north-east winds home in winter.

Map: the world in AD 300.back: **Diocletian's** (284–305) system of **four emperors** sharing the Roman frontiers.
Capital of the **Sasanian Persians** (from 224), on the **Tigris** near modern Baghdad.
The great **faiths win whole states**; **Rome splits** (the East goes on); **Islam's empire** from Spain to the Indus; **China reunites** under Sui and Tang.

Constantine and Christian Rome, 312–451.back: **28 October 312**, outside Rome: **Constantine** defeats Maxentius, after a sign from the Christian God, by his own account.
**325**: Constantine's council of bishops on the teachings of **Arius**.
**380**: **Theodosius I** makes Nicene Christianity the faith of the empire; pagan sacrifice banned **391–392**.

Constantine and Christian Rome, 312–451.front: Why did the Council of Chalcedon (451) matter so much?
Constantine and Christian Rome, 312–451.back: Much of **Egypt, Syria and Armenia** rejected its definition and formed **separate churches**, so the Christian East was divided when Islam arrived.

Goths, Huns and the sack of Rome, 376–45.back: **9 August 378**: Goths destroy a Roman army and kill the emperor **Valens**.
**24 August 410**: the Goths sack Rome for three days; Augustine answers with ***The City of God***.
Ruler of the **Huns** about **445–453**; checked at the **Catalaunian Plains (451)**; died **453**.

Goths, Huns and the sack of Rome, 376–45.front: Why did the Vandal capture of Carthage (439) hurt the West so badly?
Goths, Huns and the sack of Rome, 376–45.back: **Africa was the West's richest province**: losing its taxes and grain meant the western emperors **could no longer pay armies**.

476: did Rome fall?.back: General who deposed the last western emperor **Romulus Augustulus** in **476** and ruled Italy as king.

476: did Rome fall?.front: Why do many historians say Rome did not fall in 476?
476: did Rome fall?.back: **The Eastern Roman Empire went on** from Constantinople until **1453**; its people called themselves **Romans**. What ended was Roman government **in the West**.

476: did Rome fall?.front: Decline and fall or transformation: the two sides
476: did Rome fall?.back: **Ward-Perkins/Heather**: real collapse, of living standards and of the state, under outside pressure. **Brown/Goffart**: a creative **late antiquity** and an accommodation. Regional archaeology helps decide.

The Gupta golden age, about 320–550.back: Gupta king about **375–415**; conquered western India; Faxian visited in his reign.
Mathematician-astronomer; ***Aryabhatiya*** (**499**): π ≈ **3.1416**, the Earth turning on its axis.
Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled India about **399–412**.

The Gupta golden age, about 320–550.front: Why is the Gupta 'golden age' label disputed?
The Gupta golden age, about 320–550.back: The **culture** was brilliant, but critics (**R. S. Sharma, Thapar**) say the glory was the **courts' and Brahmins'**, while land grants and caste rules bore harder on others.

Teotihuacan and the Classic Maya kings,.front: Teotihuacan at its height, and its burning
Teotihuacan and the Classic Maya kings,.back: City near Mexico City; **Pyramid of the Sun**; perhaps **100,000+** people about 400–550; centre **burned about 550**.
**January 378**: **Siyaj K'ak'**, tied to Teotihuacan, reaches Tikal and a new dynasty is installed.

Teotihuacan and the Classic Maya kings,.front: Why can the Classic Maya be studied as history, not only archaeology?
Teotihuacan and the Classic Maya kings,.back: **Maya script was largely deciphered** from the 1950s to the 1990s, so stelae give **named kings, dates and wars**.

The Germanic kingdoms: Ostrogoths, Visig.back: Ruled **Italy 493–526** from **Ravenna**, keeping the Senate and Roman officials.
**587**: the Visigothic king turns from Arian to **Catholic**; confirmed at Toledo, **589**.

The Germanic kingdoms: Ostrogoths, Visig.front: Why did conversion from Arian to Catholic matter to the Germanic kings?
The Germanic kingdoms: Ostrogoths, Visig.back: It **ended the religious gap** with their Roman subjects, letting rulers and ruled **merge** into one people.

Clovis and the Merovingian Franks, 481–7.back: Frankish king about **481–511**; baptised a **Catholic** (between **496 and 508**); won at **Vouillé, 507**; capital Paris.
Bishop (about **538–594**) whose *Histories* are the main source on the Merovingian Franks.
**732**: **Charles Martel** defeats an Umayyad army from Spain; a raid or an invasion is debated.
Chief officials who held real power under the late Merovingians; **Pippin III** took the crown in **751**.

Justinian, Theodora and the Roman reconq.back: **January 532**, Constantinople: Blues and Greens revolt; crushed by **Belisarius** in the Hippodrome.
**529–534**: Justinian's edition of Roman law, later the **basis of continental European law**.
Built **532–537** by Anthemius and Isidore; the largest church in the world for nearly **a thousand years**.
**541–542**: bubonic plague (*Yersinia pestis*, confirmed by ancient DNA); its death toll is **disputed**.

The Sasanian Persian empire, 224–651.back: King **531–579**: tax reform, a paid army; remembered as the **model just king**.
**642**: the last great Persian army defeated by the Arabs; **Yazdegerd III** killed near Merv, **651**.

The Sui reunite China and the Tang build.back: Built under **Sui Yangdi** (main sections about **605–611**), linking the **Yellow River and the Yangtze**.
Ruled as emperor of her own Zhou dynasty, **690–705**: the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name.
Tang capital (modern **Xi'an**): a walled grid of **108 wards**, home to Sogdians, Persians, Koreans and Japanese.

The Sui reunite China and the Tang build.front: Why is the Sui compared to the Qin?
The Sui reunite China and the Tang build.back: Both were **short, harsh dynasties** that reunified China and **built what a longer dynasty** (Han, Tang) then used.

The last war of antiquity: Rome against.back: Roman emperor **610–641**; invaded Persia and won at **Nineveh, December 627**.
**614**: the city taken and the **True Cross** carried to Persia; restored by Heraclius about **630**.

The last war of antiquity: Rome against.front: Why did the war of 602–628 make the Arab conquests easier?
The last war of antiquity: Rome against.back: It left **both empires exhausted**, their treasuries empty and their cities sacked; Persia fell into **civil war**.

Arabia before Islam and the life of Muha.back: **622**: Muhammad's emigration from Mecca to **Yathrib (Medina)**; **year 1 of the Islamic calendar**.
Author (died about **767**) of the first full biography of Muhammad, surviving in **Ibn Hisham**'s edition.
Parchment radiocarbon-dated to **about 568–645**: evidence that the text is early.

Arabia before Islam and the life of Muha.front: The debate over the sources for Muhammad's life
Arabia before Islam and the life of Muha.back: The biographies are **two centuries later**. **Sceptics** (Wansbrough, Crone and Cook) doubt them; **others** (Donner) point to early manuscripts and documents supporting the core.

The Rashidun caliphs and the Arab conque.back: **August 636**: an Arab army destroys the Roman army in **Syria**.
**Basra, Kufa, Fustat**: where the Arab conquerors lived apart from the conquered.

The Rashidun caliphs and the Arab conque.front: Why did the conquered lands stay mostly non-Muslim for a century or more?
The Rashidun caliphs and the Arab conque.back: Conquest offered **protected status** for a tax, not forced conversion; majorities became Muslim only **over the next three centuries**.

The Rashidun caliphs and the Arab conque.front: How did the Sunni–Shi'a division begin?
The Rashidun caliphs and the Arab conque.back: As a dispute over **political succession**: the Shi'a held leadership belonged to **Ali and his descendants**.

Monks and missionaries: Ireland, Iona an.back: Written by **Benedict of Nursia** (Monte Cassino, about **529**); the pattern of Western monasteries for a thousand years.
Sent by **Pope Gregory the Great**; reached **Kent in 597**; first archbishop of Canterbury.
**664**: Northumbria adopts the **Roman** dating of Easter over the Irish.
English missionary to Germany; felled **Donar's oak** at Geismar (**723**); killed in Frisia, **754**.

Primary source: Bede and the sparrow in.back: Monk of **Jarrow** (about **673–735**); finished the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* in **731**.
**627**, Northumbria: Edwin's nobles debate Christianity; the **sparrow through the hall** speech.

Primary source: Bede and the sparrow in.front: Why might the sparrow speech be Bede's own words?
Primary source: Bede and the sparrow in.back: He wrote **about 104 years later**, the speaker is **unnamed**, and ancient historians often **composed fitting speeches**; it may still keep a real memory.

The Umayyad caliphate from Damascus, 661.back: **10 October 680**: **Husayn**, grandson of Muhammad, killed by an Umayyad army; central to **Shi'i memory**.
Jerusalem, **691–692**, under **Abd al-Malik**: one of the first great monuments of Islam.
**January 750**: the **Abbasids** defeat the last Umayyad caliph.

The Umayyad caliphate from Damascus, 661.front: Why did the Umayyads lose support?
The Umayyad caliphate from Damascus, 661.back: They favoured **Arabs**: non-Arab converts (**mawali**) paid more and got less, and Shi'is, Kharijites and Berbers all opposed them.

Silla's Korea and Japan from Nara to Hei.back: Korean kingdom **668–935**, after defeating Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668) with Tang help, then expelling the Tang by **676**.
Modern **Kyoto**, capital from **794**; the age of the **Fujiwara** regents and *The Tale of Genji*.
