Silla's Korea and Japan from Nara to Hei.front: Why did Heian women write so much of Japan's early prose?
Silla's Korea and Japan from Nara to Hei.back: The **kana** syllabaries let Japanese be written by sound, and women, less expected to write in **Chinese**, used them.

India after the Guptas: Harsha, the Chal.back: Ruled north India from **Kanauj**, **606–647**; known from **Bana** and **Xuanzang**.
Cut from a single hillside under the **Rashtrakuta** king **Krishna I** (about **756–773**).
Devotional worship of a personal God, sung in **Tamil** by the **Nayanars and Alvars** (about **500s–800s**).

Al-Andalus: from the conquest of 711 to.back: Berber commander who crossed to Spain in **711**; **Gibraltar** (*Jabal Tariq*) is named after him.
Ruler of al-Andalus **912–961**; declared himself **caliph** at **Córdoba** in **929**.

Al-Andalus: from the conquest of 711 to.front: The convivencia debate: the two sides
Al-Andalus: from the conquest of 711 to.back: **Menocal**: a remarkable shared culture of three faiths. **Fernández-Morera**: a **hierarchy** with real violence. **When and where you look**, and against what standard, decides much.

Talas, An Lushan and the fall of the Tan.back: **751**, Central Asia: **Tang** v. **Abbasids**; the Tang routed when the **Karluks** change sides.
**755–763**: a frontier general takes both Tang capitals; ended with **Uyghur** help.

Talas, An Lushan and the fall of the Tan.front: Why is the Tang census drop after 755 not a death toll?
Talas, An Lushan and the fall of the Tan.back: From **53 million (754) to 17 million (764)**, it shows the state's **loss of registration** as well as real deaths.
The **oldest dated printed book**, found in the cave library at **Dunhuang**.

The Abbasids, Baghdad and the House of W.back: **762**, by the caliph **al-Mansur**: a **round city** on the Tigris.
Baghdad scholar (about **780–850**): his book gave us **algebra**; his name gives **algorithm**.
**869–883**: enslaved East Africans in southern Iraq rise and hold the region for **fourteen years**.

The Abbasids, Baghdad and the House of W.front: What was the House of Wisdom, and why is it debated?
The Abbasids, Baghdad and the House of W.back: The ***Bayt al-Hikma*** of al-Ma'mun: an academy, or (Gutas) a **palace library**, with translation driven by **many patrons**. The **translation movement** itself is not in doubt.

Charlemagne and the Carolingian empire,.back: **25 December 800**, St Peter's, Rome: crowned **emperor** by Pope **Leo III**.
The clear script of Charlemagne's scribes, **ancestor of our lower-case letters**.
**843**: Charlemagne's empire split in three, the roots of **France and Germany**.
**955**: **Otto I** crushes the Magyars; crowned emperor in **962**.

Byzantine Iconoclasm and the Macedonian.back: The great Umayyad siege, beaten off with walls, fleet and **Greek fire**.
**843**: the empress **Theodora** restores icons for good, ending Iconoclasm.

Byzantine Iconoclasm and the Macedonian.front: Why do Brubaker and Haldon doubt the traditional story of Iconoclasm?
Byzantine Iconoclasm and the Macedonian.back: The sources for **Leo III**'s iconoclasm were written **later by its enemies**; the policy may really have begun under **Constantine V**.

Srivijaya, Borobudur and the first Angko.back: Malay sea power centred at **Palembang, Sumatra** (about **650–1100s**), controlling the **Strait of Malacca**.
Buddhist stepped monument in central **Java**, built by the **Sailendras** about **780–830**.
Proclaimed universal monarch on **Mount Kulen** in **802**: founder of the Khmer empire of **Angkor**.
Ship sunk about **830** off Sumatra with some **60,000** pieces of Tang pottery: the China–Persian Gulf sea route.

Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade.back: **Soninke** empire of the Sahel (southern Mauritania and western Mali); in Arab sources from the **late 700s**; capital probably **Koumbi Saleh**.
Geographer of Córdoba whose **1068** account describes Ghana's two towns and the king's gold.

Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade.front: How did Ghana grow rich on gold it did not mine?
Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade.back: The goldfields (**Bambuk, Bure**) lay to the south; Ghana **controlled and taxed the trade** between miners and desert merchants, and **kept the nuggets** for the king.

Aksum's decline, Christian Nubia and the.back: King of **Aksum** who converted to Christianity in the **330s–340s**; his coins bear the **cross**.
**652** treaty between Christian **Nubia** (Makuria) and Muslim Egypt; held about **600 years**.
Swahili town in the **Lamu islands** from about **750**, with timber mosques from the late 700s.
Not Arab colonists: **Bantu-speaking Africans**, growing from local villages, with deep **Indian Ocean** ties.

The Classic Maya collapse, about 750–950.back: **909**, at **Toniná**: the end of the southern Maya monument tradition.
Maya city burned and abandoned in haste about **810**, its houses left full of goods.

The Classic Maya collapse, about 750–950.front: Why doesn't drought alone explain the Maya collapse?
The Classic Maya collapse, about 750–950.back: The **drier north flourished** at the same time; most historians see **drought, war, environmental strain and political failure** working together.

Tiwanaku and Wari: the Andean empires be.back: City near **Lake Titicaca**, Bolivia, at about **3,850 m**; flourished about **500–1000**; **Gateway of the Sun**.
Highland state of central **Peru** (about **600–1000**), capital near **Ayacucho**; roads and centres such as **Pikillacta**.

The Viking age, 793–1000.back: **793**: the first great Viking raid on England.
**878**: **Alfred the Great** defeats the Great Army; England split with the **Danelaw**.
Norse site in **Newfoundland**; tree rings show wood cut in **1021**: Europeans in America ~500 years before Columbus.
Abbasid envoy who met **Rus'** traders on the **Volga** in **921–922** and described a ship cremation.

Kievan Rus' and the baptism of 988.back: Brothers from Thessalonica, missionaries to **Moravia** from **863**; created the **Glagolitic** alphabet for Slavonic.
History compiled at **Kyiv** about **1113**; tells of **Rurik (862)** and Vladimir's choice of faith.
**988** (sources give 987–989): the prince of Kyiv baptised and married to **Anna**, sister of **Basil II**.
Were the **Rus'** Scandinavians or Slavs? Most now agree: a ruling group of **largely Scandinavian origin** that quickly became **Slavic**.

The Polynesian voyages and the Austrones.back: Replica voyaging canoe that sailed **Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976** without instruments, guided by **Mau Piailug**.
Re-dating (**Wilmshurst, 2011**) puts the Society Islands at **about 1025–1120**, then a fast spread to **Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand** (about 1250–1300).

The Polynesian voyages and the Austrones.front: How do we know Polynesians met Americans?
The Polynesian voyages and the Austrones.back: The American **sweet potato** grew in East Polynesia before Europeans, and **DNA** shows Native American ancestry dating to about **1150–1230**.
The language of **Madagascar**, closest to **Ma'anyan** of southern **Borneo**.

Connections: the world in AD 1000.back: **Conquest** (Arab armies, Charlemagne), **kings choosing** (Clovis, Vladimir), and **merchants and monks** along trade routes.
Rome **continued in the East**, Persia became part of the **Islamic world**, China was **reunited and divided again**; most of Eurasia now **Christian, Muslim or Buddhist**.
Turkish dynasty, converted to Islam; took **Baghdad in 1055**, beat Byzantium at **Manzikert, 1071**.

Map: the world in the year 1000.back: **Abbasids** in Baghdad (figureheads under the Buyids), **Fatimids** in Cairo (from **969**), **Umayyads** of Córdoba (breaking up after **1009**).

Map: the world in the year 1000.front: The richest cities of the year 1000
Map: the world in the year 1000.back: **Kaifeng**, **Constantinople**, **Baghdad** and **Córdoba** — all **outside Latin Europe**: in 1000 there was no single centre of the world.

The Great Schism of 1054.back: Cardinal **Humbert** lays a bull excommunicating Patriarch **Michael Cerularius** on the altar of **Hagia Sophia**.
"And the Son": the Western **addition to the Creed**, rejected by the East. One of the quarrels behind 1054.

The Great Schism of 1054.front: Was 1054 the real break between East and West?
The Great Schism of 1054.back: The traditional date, but **contemporaries barely noticed**; many historians see the split as gradual, made lasting by the **sack of 1204**. Excommunications **lifted in 1965**.

The Seljuk Turks and the battle of Manzi.back: Seljuk leader who entered **Baghdad in 1055** and took the title **sultan**: the caliph reigned, the sultan ruled.
**26 August 1071**, eastern Anatolia: **Alp Arslan** defeats and captures Emperor **Romanos IV Diogenes**.

The Seljuk Turks and the battle of Manzi.front: Why did Byzantium lose Anatolia after 1071?
The Seljuk Turks and the battle of Manzi.back: Less the battle than **ten years of civil war** after it, while Turkish bands spread unopposed; by **1081** most of Anatolia was gone.
Seljuk state in Anatolia, first at **Nicaea** (about 1080), later **Konya**.

The First Crusade and the crusader state.back: **November 1095**: **Urban II** preaches an armed pilgrimage that counts as **penance**.
**15 July 1099**: taken by the First Crusade, followed by a **massacre** of Muslims and Jews.

The First Crusade and the crusader state.front: Why did the First Crusade succeed?
The First Crusade and the crusader state.back: The Muslim Near East was **divided**: Seljuk princes against each other, and the **Fatimids** rivals of the Seljuks.

The First Crusade and the crusader state.front: Why do many historians think crusaders went for faith, not loot?
The First Crusade and the crusader state.back: Their charters show them **selling or mortgaging land** to pay; many came home poorer. **Penance** explains the cost.

Saladin, the Third Crusade and the end o.back: **4 July 1187**, near the Sea of Galilee: **Saladin** destroys the army of Jerusalem; the city surrenders **2 October 1187**.
**1192**, ending the Third Crusade: Jerusalem stays with Saladin; **Christian pilgrims may visit**.
Taken by the **Mamluks**: the **end of the crusader states**.

The Fourth Crusade and the sack of Const.back: Old, nearly blind **doge of Venice** who led the Fourth Crusade's fleet, first to **Zara (1202)**, then **Constantinople**.
**12–13 April 1204**, three days of plunder by the Fourth Crusade; a **Latin Empire** ruled until **1261**.

The Fourth Crusade and the sack of Const.front: The Fourth Crusade: accident or plot?
The Fourth Crusade and the sack of Const.back: **Chain of accidents** (Queller and Madden: debt, Alexios's promises, his murder) or a **Venetian and German agenda**. No private agreements survive to decide it.

Lords, vassals and peasants: the argumen.back: Land or income granted **in return for service**; Latin *feodum*, the root of "feudal".
A peasant **bound to the land**, owing labour and dues; not a slave who could be sold.

Lords, vassals and peasants: the argumen.front: Why do some historians reject the word "feudalism"?
Lords, vassals and peasants: the argumen.back: It is a **17th–18th-century coinage**; Elizabeth **Brown (1974)** and Susan **Reynolds (1994)** argued it forces varied arrangements into **one false model**.

Towns, merchants and guilds in medieval.back: German trading towns led by **Lübeck**, dominating Baltic and North Sea trade from the **1200s**.
North-eastern France: **the hub of European trade** in the 12th and 13th centuries, where Italian and Flemish merchants met.
Leonardo of Pisa, whose book of **1202** introduced **Hindu-Arabic numerals** to Italian merchants.

Towns, merchants and guilds in medieval.front: How did a medieval guild work?
Towns, merchants and guilds in medieval.back: It set **prices and quality**, trained **apprentices → journeymen → masters**, limited competition, and supported members' widows.

Popes against kings: from Canossa to Avi.back: **January 1077**: **Henry IV** stands three days in the snow as a penitent before **Gregory VII**.
**1122** compromise: the Church invests bishops with **ring and staff**; the emperor with their **lands**.
**1309–77**: seven French popes at Avignon; Petrarch's "**Babylonian captivity**".
**1414–18**: ends the **Western Schism** of rival popes; burns **Jan Hus** (1415).

The first universities and the recovery.back: Latin for a **corporation or guild**: a university was a guild of masters or students.
Translator at **Toledo** (died **1187**) of dozens of Arabic works, including Ptolemy and **Ibn Sina's Canon**.
Dominican at Paris (about 1225–74); his ***Summa Theologiae*** reconciled **Aristotle** with Christian teaching.

The first universities and the recovery.front: Did the university borrow from the madrasa?
The first universities and the recovery.back: **Makdisi (1981)**: close parallels in licence, disputation and college. Others: the **chartered self-governing corporation** is new. No proven line of transmission.

The Hundred Years' War, 1337–1453.front: Why did the Hundred Years' War begin?
The Hundred Years' War, 1337–1453.back: **Edward III** claimed the French crown through his mother (**1328**), and Philip VI confiscated **Gascony** (**1337**).
**25 October 1415**: **Henry V** defeats the French; leads to the **Treaty of Troyes (1420)**.
Relieved **Orléans (1429)**, saw Charles VII crowned at **Reims**; **burned at Rouen, 30 May 1431**.
**17 July 1453**: French cannon end the war; England keeps only **Calais**.

Song China: the richest state on earth,.back: **1127**: the **Jurchen Jin** take **Kaifeng** and capture two emperors; the Song move south to **Hangzhou**.
Fast-ripening rice from today's Vietnam, spread by the Song state from **1012**.
Sichuan paper certificates; the Song state issued them from the **1020s**: the **first government paper money**.

Song China: the richest state on earth,.front: The "Song economic revolution": for and against
Song China: the richest state on earth,.back: **For** (Elvin): money, markets, iron and output centuries ahead of Europe. **Against**: shaky figures, and growth from settling the south more than new production.

Printing, gunpowder and the compass in S.back: Made **movable type of baked clay** in the **1040s**, recorded by Shen Kuo (**1088**).
Korean Buddhist text of **1377**: the **oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type**.
Song military manual of **1044** with the **first written gunpowder formulas**.

Printing, gunpowder and the compass in S.front: Why did movable type matter less in China than in Europe?
Printing, gunpowder and the compass in S.back: Chinese needs **thousands of characters**, so carving whole **woodblocks** was often as cheap; woodblocks stayed dominant until the 19th century.

Japan's shoguns: Kamakura and Ashikaga,.back: Victor of the Genpei War (**Dan-no-ura, 1185**); founded the **Kamakura** shogunate; shogun **1192**.
"Divine wind": the storms that wrecked the Mongol fleets of **1274** and **1281**.
Turned on Emperor Go-Daigo; **shogun from 1338**, ruling from **Muromachi** in Kyoto.

The Khmer Empire and the city of Angkor.back: Built under **Suryavarman II** (r. 1113–about 1150), dedicated to **Vishnu**; its towers stand for **Mount Meru**.
Buddhist Khmer king (r. **1181–about 1218**); built **Angkor Thom** and the **Bayon**.
Several causes together: **war with Ayutthaya** (sack **1431**), **droughts and floods** in tree rings, the shift to **Theravada**, and trade moving to the coast.

The Delhi Sultanate, 1206–1398.back: **1192**: **Muhammad of Ghor** defeats **Prithviraj Chauhan** and takes Delhi.
Former slave, **first sultan of Delhi (1206)**; began the **Qutb Minar**.
Sultan (r. **1296–1316**) who **beat off the Mongols** and fixed Delhi's market prices.

The Delhi Sultanate, 1206–1398.front: Eaton's reading of temple destruction in the sultanate
The Delhi Sultanate, 1206–1398.back: About **80** documented cases (1192–1760), real but aimed at **royal temples of enemy kings**: politics more than a war on Hinduism.

Temüjin becomes Genghis Khan, 1162–1227.front: The Secret History of the Mongols
Temüjin becomes Genghis Khan, 1162–1227.back: Mongol court epic, written **after Genghis's death** (from 1228 to the 1250s): the main source for his early life.
Assembly on the **Onon** that proclaimed Temüjin **Chinggis Khan**.

Temüjin becomes Genghis Khan, 1162–1227.front: How did Genghis Khan reorganise the Mongols?
Temüjin becomes Genghis Khan, 1162–1227.back: A **decimal army** (10s to 10,000s) mixing tribes, so loyalty went to the khan; a **guard** of 10,000; promotion by merit.
**1218**: a Khwarazmian governor kills a Mongol caravan, triggering the invasion of **1219–21**.

The Mongol conquests and the four khanat.back: **11 April 1241**: the Mongols destroy the Hungarian army.

The Mongol conquests and the four khanat.front: Why did the Mongols leave Hungary in 1242?
The Mongol conquests and the four khanat.back: **Ögedei's death** (succession), a **cold wet spring** that ruined pasture (tree rings, 2016), and heavy losses. No Mongol source decides it.

The sack of Baghdad, 1258, and Ain Jalut.back: **10 February 1258**: Hülegü takes the city; the caliph **al-Musta'sim** is executed. The death toll is **unknown**.
**3 September 1260**, Galilee: the **Mamluks** under Qutuz and **Baybars** defeat the Mongols.
Founded **1259** by **Hülegü** for the astronomer **Nasir al-Din al-Tusi**.

Pax Mongolica: roads, relay posts and a.back: The Mongol **relay network of post stations** for official messengers.
A Mongol tablet of gold, silver or wood carried **as a passport**.
Turkic Christian monk from near Beijing; envoy of the Ilkhan to **Rome and Paris, 1287–88**.
**For** (Allsen): deliberate movement of goods, people and ideas. **Against**: bought with **vast destruction**, and the khanates fought each other.

Kublai Khan and Yuan China, 1271–1368.back: Kublai's capital on the site of **Beijing**; the dynasty named **Yuan** in **1271**.
**1268–73**: ended by **counterweight trebuchets** built by Muslim engineers; opened the Song south.
**Trần Hưng Đạo** of Đại Việt destroys a Mongol fleet on **hidden stakes**.
Succession struggles, **Yellow River floods (1340s)**, worthless **paper money**, and the **Red Turban** rising (from 1351); **Zhu Yuanzhang** took Dadu in **1368**.

The Golden Horde and the rise of Moscow.back: Capital of the **Golden Horde**, on the lower **Volga**.
The khan's **patent to rule**, which Rus' princes had to fetch from the Horde.
"Moneybag": prince of Moscow who **collected the tribute for the khan**, and kept some.
**1380**: **Dmitry Donskoy** of Moscow defeats a Horde army; Moscow is burned in **1382**.

Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta: two travelle.back: Romance writer who wrote up **Marco Polo's** story in a Genoese prison, about **1298**.

Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta: two travelle.front: Did Marco Polo go to China?
Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta: two travelle.back: **Wood (1995)**: no Great Wall, tea or chopsticks. **Vogel (2013)**: accurate detail on **paper money and salt**. Most specialists: **he went**.
Ibn Battuta's "journey", dictated at Fez in **1355–56** to **Ibn Juzayy**.

Mali: Sundiata and Mansa Musa.back: About **1235**: **Sundiata** defeats **Sumanguru** of Sosso and founds Mali.
**1324**: through **Cairo** to Mecca; **al-Umari** says his gold lowered its value in Cairo.
**Timbuktu**, about **1327**, credited to **al-Sahili**, brought back by Mansa Musa.

Mali: Sundiata and Mansa Musa.front: How do we know Sundiata existed?
Mali: Sundiata and Mansa Musa.back: The griots' **oral epic**, confirmed independently by **Ibn Khaldun**, who names a conqueror **Mari Jata**.

Primary source: Ibn Battuta judges Mali,.back: Musa's brother, king of Mali (about **1341–60**), Ibn Battuta's host in **1352–53**.

Primary source: Ibn Battuta judges Mali,.front: What does Ibn Battuta praise in Mali?
Primary source: Ibn Battuta judges Mali,.back: "**Complete security**" on the roads, **abhorrence of injustice**, and protection of **dead foreign merchants' property** for their heirs.

Primary source: Ibn Battuta judges Mali,.front: Why read Ibn Battuta on Mali with care?
Primary source: Ibn Battuta judges Mali,.back: He judges by **Moroccan Islamic law**; what he calls bad is evidence of **Mande customs kept alongside Islam**; and the text was **dictated three years later**.

Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe.back: Hilltop capital at the **Limpopo–Shashe** confluence, about **1220–1290**; the **golden rhinoceros**.
Great Zimbabwe's curving **mortarless granite wall**, up to about **11 m** high.

Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe.front: Who built Great Zimbabwe, and how was it shown?
Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe.back: **Ancestors of the Shona**; shown by **Randall-MacIver (1905)** and **Caton-Thompson (1929)** against colonial claims of foreign builders.

The Swahili coast: Kilwa and the monsoon.back: Island city off southern Tanzania, rich in the **1300s** from controlling the **Sofala gold** trade.
Cliff-top palace at **Kilwa**, about the **1320s–30s**, built by **al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman**.

The Swahili coast: Kilwa and the monsoon.front: How does the monsoon shape Indian Ocean trade?
The Swahili coast: Kilwa and the monsoon.back: North-east winds (about Nov–Mar) carry ships **to Africa**; south-west winds (about Apr–Sep) carry them **back**: one round trip a year.

The Swahili coast: Kilwa and the monsoon.front: Swahili origins: what did the 2023 DNA study find?
The Swahili coast: Kilwa and the monsoon.back: About **half African, half Asian** (mostly **Persian**) ancestry from about **1000**: African mothers, incoming Asian fathers. **An African society that absorbed newcomers**.

Ethiopia: Lalibela's churches and the So.back: St George's at **Lalibela**: a **cross-shaped church cut down from solid rock**.
"Glory of the Kings", compiled in Ge'ez in the **early 14th century**: the Solomonic dynasty's claim to descend from **Solomon and the Queen of Sheba**.
Overthrew the **Zagwe** in **1270** and founded the **Solomonic dynasty**, which lasted (with breaks) to **1974**.

Cahokia and the peoples of North America.back: **Cahokia**, Illinois: about **30 m** high, the largest earthwork in the Americas north of Mexico.
Great house at **Chaco Canyon** (about 850–1150), with **hundreds of rooms**.
**1276–1299**, from tree rings: the Four Corners emptied as Ancestral Puebloans **migrated** south and east.

Cahokia and the peoples of North America.front: When was the Haudenosaunee confederacy founded?
Cahokia and the peoples of North America.back: **Debated**: **1142** (Mann and Fields, from an eclipse) or the **15th–16th century** (archaeology). Settled only by dating the shift to allied villages.

Tenochtitlan and the rise of the Inca.back: Mexica city on an island in **Lake Texcoco**, traditionally founded about **1325**.
**1428**: **Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan** under **Itzcoatl**: the Aztec Empire.
Inca ruler who beat the **Chanka** and began the empire, traditionally about **1438**; radiocarbon suggests expansion began earlier.
Raised fields of mud and reeds in the lake: the **food base** of Tenochtitlan.

The Black Death, 1346–1353.back: The **plague bacterium**, proven by **ancient DNA** to have caused the Black Death.
Kyrgyzstan, **1338–39**: deaths from "pestilence"; DNA (2022) ties them to the **Black Death's source strain**.

The Black Death, 1346–1353.front: How many died in the Black Death?
The Black Death, 1346–1353.back: Perhaps **30–60 per cent** of Europe, about **25–50 million**; Egypt and Syria lost a similar share.

The Black Death, 1346–1353.front: Black Death: why did wages rise in England?
The Black Death, 1346–1353.back: **Labour became scarce**; the **Statute of Labourers (1351)** tried and failed to freeze wages.

The Ming dynasty and the voyages of Zhen.back: **Zhu Yuanzhang**, peasant-born founder of the **Ming (1368)**; banned private sea trade (**1371**).
**Muslim eunuch** admiral from **Yunnan** (1371–1433); led **seven voyages, 1405–33**, as far as **Hormuz, Aden and Malindi**.

The Ming dynasty and the voyages of Zhen.front: Why did the Ming voyages stop after 1433?
The Ming dynasty and the voyages of Zhen.back: **Cost**, **officials' hostility to the eunuchs** who ran them, and the **Mongol threat** (the emperor was captured at **Tumu, 1449**).
**1409**, Sri Lanka: honours the Buddha, Allah and a Hindu god in **Chinese, Persian and Tamil**.

The rise of the Ottomans, 1300–1450.back: An **earthquake** wrecks its walls; the Ottomans occupy it: **their first foothold in Europe**.
**28 July 1402**: **Timur** destroys the Ottoman army and captures **Bayezid I**.
The levy of **Christian boys** from the Balkans, converted and trained as **Janissaries**.

The rise of the Ottomans, 1300–1450.front: The gazi thesis and its critics
The rise of the Ottomans, 1300–1450.back: **Wittek (1938)**: holy frontier warriors. **Lindner, Lowry**: pragmatic lords with Christian allies. **Kafadar (1995)**: both, in a frontier culture.

The fall of Constantinople, 1453.back: **Mehmed II** takes Constantinople; **Constantine XI** dies fighting.
Fortress Mehmed II built on the **Bosporus** in **1452** to cut the city off from the Black Sea.

The fall of Constantinople, 1453.front: How did the Ottomans get round the Golden Horn chain?
The fall of Constantinople, 1453.back: On **22 April 1453** they **dragged about 70 ships overland** behind Galata into the harbour.

The fall of Constantinople, 1453.front: Did 1453 send Greek learning to Italy?
The fall of Constantinople, 1453.back: Only in part: **Chrysoloras** taught Greek in Florence from **1397**, and **Bessarion** came in **1439**.

Connections: the world in 1450.back: Janet **Abu-Lughod (1989)**: the world of **1250–1350** as **eight trade circuits** with no single centre.
Polynesians reach **New Zealand** about **1250–1300**: the last large land settled.
Portugal: captured Africans brought for sale: **the opening of the Atlantic slave trade**.

Connections: the world in 1450.front: Evidence of Polynesian–American contact before Columbus
Connections: the world in 1450.back: Native American **DNA** in eastern Polynesians from about **1200** (2020), and the South American **sweet potato** across Polynesia.

Map: the world in 1450.back: **1449**: the Oirat Mongols destroy a Ming army and **capture the Zhengtong emperor**.

Map: the world in 1450.front: Three things true in 1450 but not in 1750
Map: the world in 1450.back: No regular contact between the **Americas and Afro-Eurasia**; **no European state held land outside Europe** (bar Portugal's toeholds); **Asia** held the richest economies.

The Italian Renaissance and the humanist.back: Study of grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry and ethics **from classical texts**, going *ad fontes*, back to the sources. Italy, about **1350–1550**.

The Italian Renaissance and the humanist.front: Lorenzo Valla and the Donation of Constantine
The Italian Renaissance and the humanist.back: In **1440** Valla showed from its Latin that the *Donation* was a **forgery** written centuries after Constantine.
**Machiavelli**'s advice to rulers, written **1513**, printed 1532: act as things are, not as they ought to be.

The Italian Renaissance and the humanist.front: Burckhardt v. Haskins on the Renaissance
The Italian Renaissance and the humanist.back: **Burckhardt** (1860): a sharp break, the birth of the modern individual. **Haskins** (1927) and medievalists: earlier revivals and **long continuity**.

Gutenberg and the printing press.back: Printed at **Mainz** about **1454–1455** with movable metal type; perhaps 160–180 copies, about **50 survive**.
Books printed **before 1501**; something like **27,000–30,000 editions** survive.
**Eisenstein** (1979): print was an **agent of change** behind the Reformation and science. **Johns** (1998): early print was piratical and unreliable; **trust in print was built slowly**.

Ming China after the treasure fleets.back: **1570s–1580s**, under Zhang Juzheng: Ming taxes and labour duties merged into **one payment in silver**.
Jesuit who reached Macau in 1582 and **Beijing in 1601**; dressed as a Confucian scholar, translated Euclid with **Xu Guangqi**.
**1592–1598**: Hideyoshi's Japan invades **Korea**; Ming armies and Admiral **Yi Sun-sin** help drive the Japanese out.

The Portuguese round Africa.back: Rounded the **Cape of Good Hope** in **1488** and landed at Mossel Bay.
Sailed Lisbon to **Calicut**, **1497–1499**; reached India in **May 1498**.

The Portuguese round Africa.front: How did the Portuguese break into the Indian Ocean trade?
The Portuguese round Africa.back: They could not outsell Asian merchants, so they used **guns on ships**, a chain of **forts**, and passes (*cartaz*) to **tax a slice** of the trade.

Columbus and 1492.back: Columbus reaches **Guanahani** in the **Bahamas**, home of the **Taíno**; he names it San Salvador.
Not the earth's shape (known to be round) but its **size**: he thought **Asia lay a short way west**.
**March 1492**: Ferdinand and Isabella order Spain's Jews to **convert or leave**.
**1507** map that first named the new continent **America**, after Amerigo Vespucci.

The conquest of Mexico, 1519–1521.back: Nahua woman, given to the Spaniards as a slave, who became **Cortés's interpreter** in Nahuatl and Maya.
**30 June – 1 July 1520**: the Spaniards flee Tenochtitlan by night with heavy losses.
**13 August 1521**, after a siege by Spaniards and **tens of thousands of Indigenous allies**; Cuauhtémoc captured.

The conquest of Mexico, 1519–1521.front: Restall's reading of the conquest of Mexico
The conquest of Mexico, 1519–1521.back: Largely an **Indigenous war won by Indigenous armies** (Tlaxcala and others), with Spaniards as partners; the Quetzalcoatl story a **post-conquest invention**.

The conquest of the Inca, 1532–1572.back: **16 November 1532**: Pizarro's ~168 men ambush the Inca court and **capture Atahualpa**.
Forest refuge of an independent Inca state from **1537** until **1572**, when **Túpac Amaru** was captured and beheaded.

The conquest of the Inca, 1532–1572.front: Why could so few Spaniards seize the Inca Empire?
The conquest of the Inca, 1532–1572.back: **Civil war** (Huáscar v. Atahualpa), **epidemics**, steel and horses, **Andean allies**, and capturing the ruler of a state built around him.
Andean author of an illustrated letter to the king of Spain, about **1615**, showing colonial abuses in nearly **400 drawings**.

The Columbian Exchange.back: Swap of **plants, animals and diseases** between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492; named by **Alfred Crosby, 1972**.

The Columbian Exchange.front: How did American crops change China?
The Columbian Exchange.back: **Maize and sweet potatoes** grew on hills unsuited to rice, helping the population reach roughly **300 million by 1800**.

The Columbian Exchange.front: How did the horse change the Great Plains?
The Columbian Exchange.back: Escaped Spanish horses let peoples such as the **Comanche** and **Lakota** build **mounted bison-hunting** ways of life by the 1700s.

The great dying in the Americas.back: From **8 million** (Kroeber) to **over 100 million** (Dobyns); a 2019 review: about **60 million**, falling to about **6 million by 1600**.
Great epidemics in Mexico in **1545** and **1576**; cause debated, one study found *Salmonella* DNA.

The great dying in the Americas.front: Virgin soil v. colonial system: the debate over the great dying
The great dying in the Americas.back: **Crosby**: disease would have caused disaster regardless. **Reséndez**, **Livi Bacci**: enslavement, overwork and dislocation **stopped recovery**.

Spain's American empire and Las Casas.back: Grant to a conqueror of the **labour and tribute** of a group of Indigenous people, in return for 'protection' and Christian teaching.
**1484–1566**; gave up his encomienda in **1514**; wrote the *Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies* (**1542**).
**1550–1551**: **Las Casas** v. **Sepúlveda**, who argued from Aristotle that some peoples were 'natural slaves'.
Forbade **enslaving Indigenous people** and ordered encomiendas to lapse; softened after settler revolt in Peru.

The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Ma.back: **1526**: Suleiman destroys the Hungarian army; King **Louis II** dies.
'The Lawgiver': the Turkish name for **Suleiman** (ruled **1520–1566**), for his law codes.
Old view: decline after Suleiman. Now: **transformation**, power shifting to viziers and elites (Tezcan, *The Second Ottoman Empire*); though it **lost wars and land from 1683**.

Safavid Iran: Ismail and Shah Abbas.back: 'Red heads': the Turkmen tribal warriors of the Safavid order, named for their **red caps**.
**1514**: Ottoman guns under **Selim I** defeat **Shah Ismail**'s cavalry.

Rwanda, 1994: the genocide against the T.back: Belgium **hardened Hutu and Tutsi into fixed racial categories**, recorded on **identity cards** from the 1930s, used at the 1994 roadblocks.
**1998–2003**, drawing in nine African states; deaths in the millions, mostly from hunger and disease (figure disputed).

South Africa's 1994 election and Africa'.back: **27 April 1994**; ANC about 62%; **Mandela inaugurated 10 May 1994**. Taught in full in the South African Politics curriculum.
Replaced the Organisation of African Unity in **2002**.
Kenyan mobile-phone money service, **2007**: phones spread across Africa faster than landlines ever had.

The internet and the digital revolution.back: English scientist at **CERN**, near Geneva, who proposed the **World Wide Web** in **1989**; the first website went online in 1991.

The internet and the digital revolution.front: Why did CERN's decision of April 1993 matter?
The internet and the digital revolution.back: It put the web's software **in the public domain**, so the web grew as an **open network**, not one company's product.
US Defense Department network, first linked in **1969**; the root of the internet.
Launched by Apple in **2007**; the start of the smartphone era.

9/11 and the war in Afghanistan.back: Al-Qaeda hijackers crash four airliners into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field: **2,977 killed**.
Saudi leader of **al-Qaeda**; sheltered by the Taliban; **killed at Abbottabad, Pakistan, 2 May 2011**.
**15 August 2021**: the Taliban enter Kabul as US forces withdraw under the **Doha Agreement** (February 2020).

9/11 and the war in Afghanistan.front: Name four readings of why the Afghan war failed
9/11 and the war in Afghanistan.back: **Mission drift** to state-building; **Pakistan's sheltering** of the Taliban; the **diversion to Iraq**; **corruption** in the Afghan state.

The Iraq War, 2003–2011.back: US-led forces cross from Kuwait on **20 March 2003**, with **no new UN resolution** authorising force; Baghdad falls 9 April.
US Iraq Survey Group, **September 2004**: Iraq had **destroyed its stockpiles in 1991** and had no active WMD programmes by 2003.

The Iraq War, 2003–2011.front: Why do estimates of Iraqi war deaths differ so widely?
The Iraq War, 2003–2011.back: **Method**: counting documented deaths (Iraq Body Count, **over 200,000** civilians) versus extrapolating from household surveys (about 150,000 to over 600,000 by 2006).
**June 2014**: heir of al-Qaeda in Iraq declares a "caliphate" across Iraq and Syria.

The rise of China.back: **January–February 1992**, to Shenzhen: restarts market reform after Tiananmen.
Launched by **Xi Jinping** in **2013**: ports, railways and loans across Asia, Africa and beyond.
**June 2020**, after the 2019 protests: ends the city's open opposition and free press.

The rise of China.front: The "peak China" debate: the two sides
The rise of China.back: Crested: **shrinking population (since 2022), debt, property slump**. Still rising: **lead in electric cars, batteries, solar, shipbuilding**.

India's growth since 1991.back: **24 July 1991**, finance minister **Manmohan Singh** under P. V. Narasimha Rao: rupee devalued, tariffs cut, the **licence raj** dismantled.
India's system of **state permits** needed to make or expand almost anything; dismantled from 1991.
The BJP under **Narendra Modi** lost its **outright majority** and governs in coalition.

The 2008 financial crisis.back: **15 September 2008**: the largest bankruptcy in US history; the crisis turns global.
A US home loan to a borrower **who could not easily repay**; bundled into securities sold worldwide.
The **$700 billion** US bank rescue passed by Congress in **October 2008**.

The 2008 financial crisis.front: How did 2008 feed the politics of the 2010s?
The 2008 financial crisis.back: **Banks were rescued while millions lost homes and jobs**, and few bankers were prosecuted: an anger many trace to Occupy, the Tea Party and populism (how much is contested).

The Arab Spring and the war in Syria.back: Tunisian street vendor who set himself on fire at **Sidi Bouzid, 17 December 2010**; the spark of the Arab Spring.
**11 February 2011**, after eighteen days of protest in Cairo's **Tahrir Square**.
**8 December 2024**: rebels led by **Hayat Tahrir al-Sham** take Damascus; Assad flees to Moscow.

The Arab Spring and the war in Syria.front: Why did most Arab Spring uprisings fail? Four readings
The Arab Spring and the war in Syria.back: Armies and security services **outlasted** protesters; **outside powers** made proxy wars; **no organisations ready to govern**; the **economic grievances** were never solved.

Russia under Putin.back: Russian deals of **1995–96** by which a few insiders, the **oligarchs**, gained huge state companies cheaply.
**31 December 1999**, on Yeltsin's resignation; elected March 2000.
Russian opposition leader; **died in an Arctic prison in February 2024**.
**Realist** (Mearsheimer): NATO expansion provoked a great power. **Internal**: one-man rule needing an enemy and an **imperial idea** that never accepted Ukraine's loss.

Ukraine: 2014 and the 2022 invasion.back: **1 December 1991**: about **90%** vote for independence, with majorities in every region.
**December 1994**: Ukraine gives up its Soviet nuclear weapons; Russia, the US and Britain pledge to respect its borders.
**March 2014**, after Russian troops without insignia seized it and a referendum held under occupation.
**24 February 2022**; Kyiv holds; Russia leaves the north by early April, leaving evidence of mass killings at **Bucha**.

Latin America since 1991: markets, the p.back: John Williamson's **1989** phrase for the reforms urged by Washington lenders: **balanced budgets, privatisation, open trade**.
The wave of **left-wing election victories** from **1998** (Chávez), including Lula in Brazil (2003) and Morales in Bolivia (2006).
Brazil's **2003** programme of cash to poor families who kept children in school; cut poverty sharply.
**3 January 2026**: US forces strike Caracas and seize Maduro, flown to New York on narco-terrorism charges; legality disputed.

Climate change as history.back: CO₂ measured at **Mauna Loa from 1958**: about **315 ppm** then, **over 420** by the mid-2020s.
**2015**: every country sets its own target; warming "well below 2 °C", pursuing **1.5 °C**.
**1997**: binding cuts for **rich countries only**; the US signed but never ratified.

Climate change as history.front: On climate, what is settled and what is debated?
Climate change as history.back: Settled: **humans are warming the Earth** (IPCC: "unequivocal"). Debated: **how fast to cut, who pays, and by what means**.

COVID-19.back: **11 March 2020**; the first cases were reported in **Wuhan** in December 2019.
WHO estimate: **14.9 million** in 2020–21 alone, against about 7 million deaths officially reported overall.

COVID-19.front: COVID's origin: the two hypotheses and what would settle it
COVID-19.back: **Natural spillover** (the Wuhan market) or **lab accident** (Wuhan Institute of Virology). Settled only by **early patient samples, lab records and animal data** from China.

Populism: the people against the elite.back: A **"thin" ideology** dividing society into **"the pure people" and "the corrupt elite"**; attaches to left or right.
**Viktor Orbán's** phrase (**2014**) for his system in Hungary, in power since 2010.

Populism: the people against the elite.front: Why populism now? The two leading explanations
Populism: the people against the elite.back: **Economic**: globalisation's losers and 2008. **Cultural backlash** (Norris and Inglehart, 2019): reaction against fast change in values. Many say both.

Primary source: the Charter of the Unite.back: Signed at **San Francisco, 26 June 1945**; in force 24 October 1945; opens **"WE THE PEOPLES OF THE UNITED NATIONS"**.
Members shall refrain from **"the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state"**.
Endorsed by UN members in **2005**: protecting populations from genocide and mass atrocity, **but only through the Security Council**.

Primary source: the Charter of the Unite.front: Why do rivals in every war since 1991 argue in the Charter's words?
Primary source: the Charter of the Unite.back: It is **the standard every government claims to meet**: an ideal, not a description.

How to read the news as history.back: Journalism, in a phrase usually credited to **Philip Graham, 1963**: valuable and **often wrong**.

How to read the news as history.front: How to read a wartime casualty claim
How to read the news as history.back: As **a fact about a claim**, not about losses: who says it, how they know, and is it **corroborated** independently?

How to read the news as history.front: Why wait before judging a breaking story?
How to read the news as history.back: The **first 48 hours** carry the most errors; early tolls for Rwanda, 9/11 and Bosnia were all later revised.

Connections: the world as of November 20.back: Hamas attacks Israel: **about 1,200 killed, about 250 taken hostage**; Israel's war in Gaza follows.
**June 2025**: Israel and Iran fight; the **US strikes Iran's nuclear sites**.

Connections: the world as of November 20.front: Which long pattern of the last five centuries is ending?
Connections: the world as of November 20.back: **The West's dominance**: Asia's share of world output is returning towards its level **before 1800**.
